Optics

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 39k Articles: 345
Optics studies light, its propagation, and instruments for forming images and measuring optical spectra.
The central question is how light carries information from a source to an observer. A useful description must explain both where the light goes and how its distribution changes. In geometrical optics, light rays locate paths and images; in physical optics, an electromagnetic wave has a wave amplitude and a wave phase, so overlapping contributions can produce wave interference and diffraction. These descriptions address different levels of detail within the same subject. [ref].
An image is especially interesting because a single object point emits light in many directions. An optical lens redirects part of that spreading bundle toward a corresponding image point; repeating this construction over the object preserves spatial information. Simply gathering more light is insufficient: light rays from distinct object points must arrive at distinct locations. This is why an optical camera needs both an optical lens and a correctly positioned receiving surface. The thin lens example below makes that correspondence quantitative. [ref].

Radiometry

Words: 4k Articles: 21
Optics OurBigBook.com
Radiometry measures the energy and power carried by electromagnetic radiation, including light. It asks how much radiation a source supplies, where it travels, and how much reaches a receiving surface. The measurements are physical rather than weighted by the sensitivity of the human eye: equal radiant fluxes at different wavelengths need not look equally bright. [ref].
The five quantities below answer different questions about the same radiation. The International System of Units makes the distinctions visible: a watt is a joule per second, while a steradian measures solid angle. [ref].
QuantityWhat is resolved?Units
Radiant flux ΦTotal radiation power in the specified beam or collectionW
Radiant intensity IPower per outgoing solid angleWsr−1
Radiance LPower per projected area and per solid angleWm−2sr−1
Irradiance EIncident power per receiving areaWm−2
Radiant exitance MOutward emitted power per emitting areaWm−2
Resolving wavelength or frequency adds a further “per unit interval”, as in spectral radiance. The notation is consistent with NIST's table of spectral quantities. In particular, radiant flux is power, whereas the existing astronomical radiative flux is power per area. [ref].
This bookkeeping makes an optical camera's collected signal calculable from a source's radiance and the geometry of the receiving aperture. It also lets radiation measurements from different instruments be compared. For example, NIST describes separate calibrations of spectral radiance and spectral irradiance for instruments used to observe Earth. [ref].

Radiant flux (Φ=dQ/dt)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Radiometry OurBigBook.com
Radiant flux is the power carried by electromagnetic radiation: radiation energy transferred per unit time, measured in watts, W=Js−1. Specify what is counted: all radiation emitted by a source, radiation within one beam, or radiation intercepted by a photodetector. Writing Q(t) for the cumulative energy crossing the specified boundary gives
Φe​(t)=dtdQ​,Φe​=t2​−t1​Q(t2​)−Q(t1​)​,Q(t2​)−Q(t1​)=∫t1​t2​​Φe​(t)dt.
(1)
The first expression is an instantaneous derivative; the second is an average over the stated time interval. If 0.020J arrives during 0.010s, the mean radiant flux is 2W. The photodetector's absorbed power equals this incident radiant flux only if it absorbs all of the incident radiation.
Keeping radiant flux fixed while widening a beam reduces its irradiance, the incident power per receiving area. Radiance additionally resolves the propagation direction and has units Wm−2sr−1; an optical camera can collect different radiant fluxes from sources with the same radiance but different apparent solid angles. Luminous flux, measured in lumens, weights the optical spectrum by the human eye's standardized response instead of counting energy equally at every wavelength. Equal radiant fluxes need not give equal luminous fluxes.[ref]
Radiant power also differs from the optical power of an optical lens, which is reciprocal focal length in dioptres. Likewise, astronomical radiative flux is power per area. Stating the units prevents these shared words from hiding different physical quantities.

Radiant flux through an oriented surface (Φnet​=Φ+​−Φ−​)

Words: 254
Radiant flux OurBigBook.com
In geometrical optics, suppose radiation has a nonnegative radiance L(x,s) whose directional contributions add as power. Here s is the actual propagation unit vector, dΩ is a solid angle element, and the collecting oriented surface A has chosen unit normal n(x). Assume the following integrals exist. The outward and inward radiant fluxes are
Φ+​=∫A​∫n⋅s>0​L(x,s)(n⋅s)dΩdA,Φ−​=∫A​∫n⋅s<0​L(x,s)(−n⋅s)dΩdA.
(2)
Both quantities are nonnegative; their difference is the signed net radiant flux. The dot product supplies the cosine of the angle with the unit normal, hence the projected area. For incoming radiation the outward unit normal gives a negative dot product; the minus sign makes the collected power positive. Measuring the incoming angle from a source-facing unit normal instead gives the familiar positive cosθ. The units check is Wm−2sr−1×m2×sr=W.
Equivalently, the incoming surface integral is Φ−​=∫A​EdA with local irradiance E; the emitted part of Φ+​ is ∫A​MdA with radiant exitance M. For a small flat patch and a narrow accepted cone, nearly constant radiance and angle give Φ≃LAcosθΔΩ. This approximation requires uniformity across the patch and cone. Direction-independent outgoing radiance over a whole hemisphere gives the different exact result Φ+​=πLA, by Lambert's cosine law and the spherical coordinates calculation in radiant exitance. Replacing the cosine-weighted integral by the hemisphere's 2π solid angle would double the answer.[ref]
These radiance formulas presume a description in additive directional power; they do not reconstruct arbitrary coherent wave interference from separate ray contributions. For general electromagnetic fields, the signed instantaneous power crossing an oriented surface is ∫A​S⋅ndA, using the Poynting vector S; optical measurements commonly average over many wave periods. A zero net radiant flux can conceal equal nonzero incoming and outgoing radiant fluxes.

Beam collection at fixed radiant flux (Φcollected​=Pmin(1,a2/b2))

Words: 230
Radiant flux OurBigBook.com
Consider an ideal parallel circular beam with uniform irradiance inside radius b, zero outside, and total radiant flux P=2W. A centred circular collector of radius a, perpendicular to the light rays, intercepts
Eb​=πb2P​,Φcollected​=Eb​πmin(a,b)2=Pmin(1,b2a2​).
(3)
For b=1cm and a=0.5cm, Eb​=20000/πWm−2≃6366.20Wm−2 and the collected radiant flux is 0.50W. Expanding the beam to b=2cm while keeping P fixed divides irradiance and the same collector's radiant flux by four: Eb​≃1591.55Wm−2 and Φcollected​=0.125W. A collector covering either entire beam still receives 2W.
Tilting a flat collector of actual area A by an angle θ to the beam direction gives Φcollected​=Eb​Acosθ if its entire projected area remains inside the uniform beam. At 60∘ the small collector's radiant flux halves. A collector large enough to intercept the whole beam after tilting still receives P: the footprint on its surface grows as 1/cosθ and cancels the irradiance factor. This model ignores diffraction, beam-edge structure, and changes in absorption with incidence angle; it counts incident rather than absorbed power.

Spectral radiant flux (Φe,λ​, Φe,ν​)

Words: 256
Radiant flux OurBigBook.com
Spectral radiant flux resolves radiant flux by wavelength or frequency:
Φe​=∫0∞​Φe,λ​(λ)dλ=∫0∞​Φe,ν​(ν)dν.
(4)
Its units are Wm−1 per metre of wavelength or WHz−1 per hertz of frequency. A density quoted per nanometre must be integrated with wavelength intervals in nanometres; its numerical value is 10−9 times the per-metre density. The frequency and wavelength spectral radiance conversion applies equally to spectral radiant flux, through the change of variables formula:
Φe,ν​(ν)=Φe,λ​(c/ν)ν2c​,
(5)
with c the speed of light in vacuum and Φe,λ​ expressed per metre. The Jacobian determinant preserves integrated power rather than the height or location of an optical spectrum's peak.
For two explicitly synthetic optical spectra, let x=λ/(1nm) and quote the following densities in mWnm−1:
fA​(x)={0.020(1−∣x−500∣/100),0,​400≤x≤600,otherwise,​fB​(x)={0.010,0,​600≤x≤800,otherwise.​
(6)
The triangle under fA​ and the rectangle under fB​ both have area 2mW: 200×0.020/2=200×0.010=2. Their band radiant fluxes differ: 450–550nm contains 1.5mW of A, while 650–750nm contains 1.0mW of B. These are specified functions, not measured source spectra.
The dark-subtracted electric current of a linear photodiode is
i=∫R(λ)Φe,λ​(λ)dλ,[R]=AW−1,
(7)
using its spectral responsivity. The figure's stipulated R gives iA​=0.60mA and iB​=1.00mA despite equal total radiant flux. Symmetry places A's mean wavelength at 500nm and B's at 700nm; a linear R averages to its value at that mean. A single electric current therefore cannot determine an unknown broadband radiant flux without additional spectral information or a sufficiently flat calibrated response.

Calibrated radiant-flux measurement

Words: 341
Radiant flux OurBigBook.com
An optical power meter makes the definition operational: collect a specified beam on a calibrated photodiode, measure its electric current, and infer incident radiant flux using spectral responsivity. In the manufacturer-authored Model 1830-R Series Optical Power Meters User's Manual by Newport Corporation, §5.5.1 specifies a concrete sequence: connect the detector and its calibration module, select watt mode and the source wavelength, block the beam and press ZERO, then unblock it and read the display. The stored background includes dark current and ambient light present during zeroing. For narrowband radiation,
Φindicated​=R(λ)iilluminated​−izero​​.
(8)
The electric current difference divided by spectral responsivity has units A/(AW−1)=W. For a stipulated R=0.40AW−1 and difference 0.20mA, the inferred radiant flux is 0.50mW; these numbers illustrate the inference and are not reported measurements. The entire beam must hit the active area, and §5.6 calls for correct wavelength, background subtraction, and operation below detector saturation. If an optical attenuator is fitted, §5.4 requires the calibrated detector–attenuator pair and the matching meter setting.
The calibration itself must connect electric current to independently known incident power. NIST's Spectroradiometric Detector Measurements: Ultraviolet, Visible, and Near-Infrared Detectors for Spectral Power by Thomas C. Larason and others describes this chain. A cryogenic radiometer, an electrical substitution radiometer, compares temperature changes from absorbed light with those from known Joule heating (§5.2). Transfer and working detectors carry that watt scale to a spectral comparator (§5.1). A source, monochromator, focusing optics, shutter, beam splitter, and monitor photodiode illuminate a standard and test detector in turn; calibrated current-to-voltage electronics and voltmeters provide the readout (§§3.2.2–3.2.4, 4.3.1). At each wavelength, subtract blocked-beam signals and normalize each detector signal by the simultaneously sampled monitor signal. Comparison with the standard yields the test detector's spectral responsivity. NIST uses two working standards and alignment normal to the beam (§6.1.1).
Controls distinguish a smaller collected radiant flux from a faulty conversion: block and unblock the beam to check the baseline; check that its footprint fits the active area; verify the calibrated optical attenuator configuration; and test proportional response within the specified operating range. Source drift faster than monitor sampling is not removed. NIST discusses finite spectral bandwidth, stray light, temperature, and spatial response variations (§§3.1.1, 6.2, 7.2). A broadband optical spectrum requires the weighted integral in spectral radiant flux, rather than dividing by an arbitrary single spectral responsivity. These limitations explain why the meter's displayed watts need a stated collection boundary, spectral assumptions, and calibration conditions.

Radiant intensity (I=dΦ/dΩ)

Words: 65
Radiometry OurBigBook.com
Radiant intensity describes how a source distributes its radiant flux over directions. A small cone of solid angle ΔΩ carries approximately IΔΩ when I varies little across it; integrating I over all emitting directions recovers the total radiant flux. For a source with isotropy emitting 4πW over a full sphere, I=1Wsr−1 and a 0.01sr cone carries 0.01W. A planar source satisfying Lambert's cosine law instead has direction-dependent radiant intensity, even though its radiance is direction-independent.

Radiance (L)

Words: 2k Articles: 10
Radiometry OurBigBook.com
Radiance resolves both position and direction: it is radiant flux per projected area and per solid angle. For a surface element of area dA, and a small outgoing cone dΩ at angle 0≤θ<π/2 to its outward unit normal,
d2Φ=L(x,s)cosθdAdΩ,[L]=Wm−2sr−1.
(9)
Here x locates the patch and s is a unit vector along the outgoing direction. The factor dAcosθ is the patch's apparent area viewed along that direction. The same local definition applies to transmitted or received radiation, choosing the positive projected area for the crossing direction. [ref].
For a planar patch of area A with spatially uniform, direction-independent radiance L, integrating over the patch gives
I(θ)=LAcosθ.
(10)
Take L=10Wm−2sr−1 and A=0.020m2. The radiant intensities are I(0)=0.20Wsr−1 and I(60∘)=0.10Wsr−1. A sufficiently narrow 0.010sr cone therefore carries approximately 2.0mW or 1.0mW, respectively. Both views have the same radiance L: the oblique view presents half the projected area. This is Lambert's cosine law, not a loss of radiance with viewing angle.
Radiance is useful because it separates a source's local directional output from the geometry of an observation. Integrating over outgoing directions gives radiant exitance; integrating incoming radiance at a receiver gives irradiance. In the stationary vacuum setting of vacuum conservation of specific intensity, a resolved uniform source retains its radiance along each light ray, while the radiant flux received from the whole source can decrease as its apparent solid angle shrinks.

Projected area (A⊥​=Acosθ)

Radiance OurBigBook.com
The projected area of a planar patch viewed from a direction is the area of its perpendicular shadow onto a plane normal to that direction. If n and s are its unit normal and viewing unit vector, then A⊥​=A∣n⋅s∣ by the dot product. On the outward side, this is Acosθ. For a rectangle tilted around one edge, the width perpendicular to that edge contracts by cosθ and the edge length stays fixed, proving the formula. At grazing view A⊥​=0; interpret the radiance definition by a limit rather than dividing by zero.

Spectral radiance (Lν​, Lλ​)

Words: 2k Articles: 8
Radiance OurBigBook.com
Spectral radiance is radiance per unit frequency or wavelength interval. Its astronomical synonym specific intensity is usually written Iν​=Lν​ or Iλ​=Lλ​; this Iν​ is a spectral radiance, distinct from the radiant intensity I in radiometry. For positive small intervals,
d3Φ=Lν​cosθdAdΩdν=Lλ​cosθdAdΩdλ.
(11)
The two expressions refer to the same spectral slice, with the positive widths related through frequency ν and wavelength λ. For frequency measured in hertz, Hz=s−1, the units are [Lν​]=Wm−2sr−1Hz−1. For wavelength measured in metres, [Lλ​]=Wm−2sr−1m−1. Integrating over a spectral band gives its radiance, and then multiplying by the collecting projected area and accepted solid angle gives a small uniform beam's radiant flux. A spectral measurement therefore retains information that the band-integrated power alone loses.
For an ideal blackbody, Planck's law gives Lν​=Bν​(T) and Lλ​=Bλ​(T) at temperature T, independent of outgoing direction. Its existing frequency and wavelength peaks of Planck's law illustrate why the coordinate matters. The simpler flat-band calculation below isolates that same change of variables without the thermal physics.
Frequency and wavelength spectral radiance conversion (Lν​=Lλ​(c/ν)c/ν2)

In vacuum, ν=c/λ, where c is the speed of light. Increasing wavelength decreases frequency, so the ordinary signed differentials satisfy dν=−cλ−2dλ. A spectral slice's positive contribution to radiance must be unchanged. The change of variables formula therefore gives the absolute Jacobian determinant
Lν​(ν)=Lλ​(c/ν)​dνdλ​​=Lλ​(c/ν)ν2c​,Lλ​(λ)=Lν​(c/λ)λ2c​.
(12)
These formulas use Lλ​ per metre and Lν​ per hertz. The factor c/ν2 has units ms=mHz−1, which converts the former density into the latter. If ℓnm​ denotes the numerical density per nanometre in Wm−2sr−1nm−1, its per-metre value is 109ℓnm​. Conversely, the per-nanometre value is 10−9 times the per-metre value. Likewise, a density per terahertz is 1012 times its per-hertz value because 1THz=1012Hz.
For a concrete stipulated spectrum, let Lλ​=C=109Wm−2sr−1m−1 between λ1​=500nm and λ2​=600nm, and zero outside. This is exactly 1Wm−2sr−1nm−1 throughout the band. Using the exact International System of Units value c=299792458ms−1, the corresponding frequency bounds are
ν1​=λ2​c​=499.654096666…THz,ν2​=λ1​c​=599.584916THz.
(13)
The transformed spectral radiance is Lν​=Cc/ν2 on this interval. At ν1​ it is approximately 1.200830743×10−12Wm−2sr−1Hz−1, and at ν2​ it is 8.339102380×10−13 in the same units. These are respectively 1.200830743 and 0.833910238 per terahertz. Thus a flat wavelength density becomes a decreasing frequency density; relabelling the horizontal axis alone would miss both the shape and the units. [ref].
The equality of band radiances has a short exact proof:
∫λ1​λ2​​Cdλ=C(λ2​−λ1​)=100Wm−2sr−1,
(14)
∫ν1​ν2​​ν2Cc​dν=Cc(ν1​1​−ν2​1​)=C(λ2​−λ1​).
(15)
The reversed bounds and the Jacobian determinant preserve the same spectral measure. Each half-band, 500–550nm and 550–600nm, carries 50Wm−2sr−1, although the corresponding frequency widths are about 54.508 and 45.423THz.
A spectrum's peak is consequently a statement about a particular density and coordinate. The frequency and wavelength peaks of Planck's law differ for precisely this reason. Integrated radiance over a specified physical band supplies a comparison that survives the change of variables.
Vacuum conservation of specific intensity
Words: 227
Spectral radiance OurBigBook.com
In a transparent, stationary vacuum with Euclidean geometry and observers at rest in the same frame, the radiative transfer equation has zero absorption and emission, so dIν​/ds=0 along a light ray. The same specific intensity reaches the observer without geometric dilution. More generally, Iν​/ν3 is a Lorentz invariant; collisionless propagation preserves this ratio along a ray even with gravitational or cosmological redshift, rather than preserving Iν​ at shifted frequencies. [ref].
The elementary geometry is instructive. Two facing surface elements separated by distance s exchange spectral radiant flux
d3Φ=Iν​s2cosθ1​cosθ2​​dA1​dA2​dν.
(16)
The receiver subtends dΩ2​=cosθ2​dA2​/s2 at the source. Describing that same traveling beam at the receiver instead uses dΩ1​=cosθ1​dA1​/s2. Both descriptions have identical geometric factors, so conservation of its radiant flux gives equal specific intensities at the two ends. This compares the same propagation direction at both ends, not emission in the opposite direction.
A uniform source remains equally bright per resolved direction under these assumptions, but occupies a smaller apparent solid angle farther away. For a small source of projected area A⊥​ at distance d and a small receiver facing it, irradiance is approximately E=LΩsource​≃LA⊥​/d2. The radiant flux intercepted by receiver area Ad​ is approximately EAd​. With L=10Wm−2sr−1, A⊥​=0.020m2 and Ad​=10−4m2, distances 10 and 20m give E≃0.002 and 0.0005Wm−2, and received radiant fluxes of 0.20 and 0.050μW. The inverse-square law concerns collected radiation from the whole source; L remains 10 at either distance.
Limb darkening
Words: 1k Articles: 5
Spectral radiance OurBigBook.com
Limb darkening is the decrease of emergent specific intensity toward the apparent edge of a stellar disc. A transit depth then depends on the intensity sampled by the planet as well as its projected area; the uniform-disc area ratio is only an approximation.
For a spherical star of radius R⋆​, let r be distance from the centre of its projected disk and let θ be the angle between the outward unit normal and the line of sight. The angular coordinate is
μ=cosθ=1−(r/R⋆​)2​.
(17)
Disk centre has μ=1; the apparent edge approaches μ=0. A resolved image measures specific intensity in each direction. Limb darkening means that this specific intensity itself falls toward the edge; the projected area factor used when collecting radiant flux is a separate geometric effect.
A simple explanation assumes a horizontally uniform plane-parallel atmosphere, a sufficiently deep optically thick medium, negligible scattering of light, and thermal absorption and emission in local thermodynamic equilibrium. Let τν​ be inward vertical optical depth at fixed frequency ν. An oblique light ray has line of sight optical depth τν​/μ, so it encounters the same attenuation at a smaller vertical optical depth. The formal solution of the radiative transfer equation gives
Iν​(0,μ)=∫0∞​Sν​(τν​)e−τν​/μμdτν​​,0<μ≤1.
(18)
Here Sν​ is the source function; under these assumptions it is the Planck function Bν​[T(τν​)]. If temperature increases inward, an oblique view preferentially samples cooler layers and hence lower specific intensity. [ref]
The weight e−τν​/μ/μ is an exponential distribution in vertical optical depth, with expected value μ and standard deviation μ. Thus “seeing down to optical depth one” refers to the line of sight, and represents a broad sampling of layers rather than a sharp emitting surface. For a source function that is linear throughout the atmosphere, the Eddington-Barbier relation is exact:
Sν​(τν​)=aν​+bν​τν​⟹Iν​(0,μ)=aν​+bν​μ=Sν​(μ).
(19)
This follows by integrating the constant and linear terms separately. A constant source function instead gives constant specific intensity, as in the blackbody limit of an isothermal atmosphere. An outward-rising temperature or important scattering of light changes the argument. Close enough to the actual edge, a plane-parallel atmosphere also loses validity because of curvature. Neither one limb-darkening coefficient nor a universal dependence on wavelength follows from this simple model.

Words: 221 Articles: 1
Limb darkening OurBigBook.com
The linear limb-darkening law parametrizes angular specific intensity by a stipulated limb-darkening coefficient u:
I(μ)=Ic​[1−u(1−μ)],Ic​=I(1),0≤u≤1.
(20)
Here I denotes specific intensity at one frequency, or radiance integrated over a specified interval of frequency or wavelength; it does not denote radiant intensity. Within this stipulated range, u=0 gives a uniform disk and I(0)/Ic​=1−u. The linear limb-darkening law is linear in μ, while its radial profile I(r)=Ic​[1−u+u1−(r/R⋆​)2​] is curved. In the linear source function example above, u=bν​/(aν​+bν​) when aν​,bν​≥0 and aν​+bν​>0.
For the illustrative choice u=0.6, the specific intensity at r/R⋆​=0, 0.8, and the limiting edge is respectively Ic​, 0.76Ic​, and 0.4Ic​. These are synthetic values, not measurements of the Sun. Real optical spectra and stellar atmospheres need not obey a linear limb-darkening law; more flexible profiles can be necessary for accurate exoplanet transit photometry. [ref]

In a spherical model with the same stellar atmosphere everywhere, the luminosity is Lν​=4πR⋆2​Fν​ and fν​=Lν​/(4πD2), consistent with the inverse-square law. Limb darkening OurBigBook.com
A dark, opaque circular planet of radius Rp​ blocks specific intensity over its overlap with the projected star. With k=Rp​/R⋆​ and no transit dilution, the instantaneous exoplanet transit depth is exactly
δ=πR⋆2​I∫overlap​IdAproj​​.
(24)
When k≪1, the entire planetary disk is inside the stellar disk, and specific intensity varies little across that disk, small-planet transit weighting reduces to
δ≃k2II(μp​)​=k21−u/31−u+uμp​​,μp​=1−z2​,z<1−k.
(25)
Here z is the projected centre separation divided by R⋆​. The numerator samples the local specific intensity; the denominator normalizes by the whole star's mean specific intensity. The small-size argument and the distinction between full overlap and ingress are explicit in the original analytic treatment. [ref]
For a short approximately straight crossing at constant transverse velocity v⊥​, write x=v⊥​t/R⋆​ with t=0 at mid-transit, and let b be the transit impact parameter. Then z2=x2+b2 and μp​=1−b2−x2​. With stipulated u=0.6 and k=0.05, a central crossing has mid-transit exoplanet transit depth approximately 0.003125, whereas b=0.8 gives 0.002375. A uniform disk would give k2=0.0025 for either fully overlapping crossing. The brighter central chord produces a deeper dip and the off-centre chord a shorter crossing at the same v⊥​.
At fixed z<1 away from the edge, a two-dimensional Taylor's theorem expansion over the symmetric planetary disk cancels the first derivatives; the first correction to the blocked radiant flux is of order k4 if the second derivatives remain bounded. This error estimate is not uniform at the edge, where the radial derivative of the linear limb-darkening law diverges. Ingress, egress, a grazing exoplanet transit, and a crossing of a starspot require the overlap integral or a suitable more complete model. Inferring k=δ​ without the local-to-mean specific intensity ratio can bias the estimated planet radius.
Solar limb-darkening drift-scan experiment
Words: 185
Limb darkening OurBigBook.com
A motivating measurement used the McMath solar optical telescope at Kitt Peak. The Sun's image drifted across a 10mm-high, 0.2mm-wide optical slit; a double-pass spectrograph selected wavelength intervals from 0.0015nm wide at 303nm to 0.007nm at 1099nm. An EMI 9750 QB photodetector or silicon photodiode supplied a digitized signal: 1kHz samples were summed into 4096 positions per crossing, including dark and off-limb sky readings. [ref]
Controls included daily realignment of optical telescope mirrors, wavelength settings between spectral lines insensitive to the rotational Doppler shift, selection of detectors without detectable hysteresis, and measured electronic nonlinearity corrections below 0.1% of maximum signal. Limb-position calibration combined centres of gravity of the edge derivative profiles with almanac semidiameters; the preliminary edge shifts were consistent with astronomical seeing of approximately 5 arcseconds full width at half maximum. [ref]
The decreasing centre-to-limb readout gives a specific intensity profile, constraining stratification of the photosphere under a radiative transfer model. Astronomical seeing, instrumental scattering of light, and solar granulation limit this inference; brightness alone does not uniquely determine temperature versus geometric height. These observations need not follow the stipulated linear limb-darkening law.

Photometry (optics)

Words: 1k Articles: 17
Optics OurBigBook.com
Photometry weights visible electromagnetic radiation by standardized visual response functions; radiometry measures its energy and power without visual weighting.[ref]
The question is how much light a source supplies under a stated visual weighting. A beam containing 1mW at the defining frequency 540THz has luminous flux 0.683lm. Moving the same radiant flux to a region of smaller spectral luminous efficacy reduces its luminous flux. Changing the optical spectrum changes this conversion even when its total power stays fixed. This makes photometry useful for comparing lighting, while radiometry remains necessary for an energy budget. The lumen counts luminous flux; the candela additionally specifies its distribution over solid angle.
Two measurement routes implement the weighting: measure an optical spectrum and evaluate a weighted integral, or use a photometer whose spectral responsivity approximates the prescribed weighting. Both require a specified collection geometry. Neither is a complete prediction of an individual's perception of a scene.[ref]

The official prescription uses linear interpolation between the specified 1 nm entries.[ref]

Lambertian reflectance is the ideal diffuse-reflection model with direction-independent outgoing radiance, the frequency-integrated specific intensity. If a fraction 0≤ρ≤1 of incident radiant flux is reflected, a surface receiving irradiance E has reflected radiance L=ρE/π. The reflected outward power per area is πL=ρE by the same hemispherical integral used for radiant exitance. Its radiant intensity still acquires the projected area factor in Lambert's cosine law.
For E=100Wm−2 and ρ=0.80, the reflected radiance is 80/π≈25.4648Wm−2sr−1. A patch of area 0.020m2 reflects 1.6W in total, and its radiant intensities at 0∘ and 60∘ are respectively 1.6/π and 0.8/πWsr−1. The radiance stays fixed as the view changes, provided the illumination stays fixed. Changing the incident angle can change irradiance and therefore the reflected radiance.

Lambert's cosine law (I(θ)=I(0)cosθ)

Words: 136
Optics OurBigBook.com
For an ideal diffuse emitting or reflecting planar surface with uniform direction-independent radiance, the radiant intensity in a direction at angle θ to its unit normal is I(θ)=I(0)cosθ. This follows immediately from I=LAcosθ and the projected area formula. The worked radiance example and diagram show the 0∘ and 60∘ cases. Lambertian reflectance supplies one physical idealization realizing the law; an ideal blackbody provides an emitting example.
The historical setting is Johann Heinrich Lambert's Photometria sive de mensura et gradibus luminis, colorum et umbrae, published in Augsburg in 1760. The screen reveals the real image; it does not create the intersection. A viewer can also see a real image without a screen if their eye receives the diverging light rays beyond the intersection. To test both image position and transverse magnification, use an optical bench with an illuminated arrow or millimetre target, a converging optical lens of nominal focal length 10cm, a movable white screen and a ruler. Measure corresponding target and image intervals, rather than guessing the whole image size when it exceeds the screen. PASCO's Experiment 12 compares distance-based and size-based magnification; the following procedure uses several object distances, as in the Northern Virginia laboratory. [ref]; [ref].
  • Align target centre, optical lens centre and screen along one optical axis, with target and screen perpendicular to it. Record bench positions of the actual target plane, optical lens plane and screen surface; distances between holder edges introduce an offset.
  • Start at u=30cm. Move the screen through the expected v=15cm region until the target's central detail is sharpest. Record u, measured v, the corresponding target and image intervals, and whether the arrow is inverted. Give the measured size ratio a negative sign if inverted.
  • Repeat at u=20cm and u=15cm. Compare the measured signed size ratio with −v/u, and calculate fest​=uv/(u+v) for each pair. The three ideal rows above are predictions to compare against, not entries to copy into the measurement record. [ref].
Keep the optical lens, illumination and central target detail fixed between trials. Approach best focus from both sides and record the interval over which sharpness is difficult to distinguish; repeat focusing to estimate its reproducibility. A modest central aperture stop tests whether peripheral light rays change the result, but also reduces brightness. Spherical aberration, chromatic aberration and diffraction can broaden the optimum; a thick optical lens also makes the chosen reference plane imperfect. Treat nominal f as an initial prediction, and report position and interval-reading limits instead of forcing exact agreement. [ref].
Moving the object toward the front optical focus from outside makes the real image larger and farther away. A failed screen search near u=f can therefore mean that the real image is beyond the bench, rather than that a virtual image has formed. At exactly u=f, the outgoing bundle from each point is parallel and no finite screen position focuses it.

An eye or a second optical lens receiving the actual outgoing light rays can nevertheless form a subsequent real image. “Virtual” describes this imaging stage, not whether the image can be seen or photographed. For a direct viewing test, bring the target to u=7.5cm, search for a sharp screen image on the outgoing side, then remove the screen and look through the optical lens toward the target. Expect an upright enlarged view if the eye receives the bundle and can focus. Record the eye position: 5cm beyond the optical lens gives a predicted apparent distance 35cm. For a position measurement, use parallax localization of a virtual image. Place a movable pencil tip or narrow comparison marker beside the apparent image, and view that marker directly beside or above the optical lens, while viewing the image through it. Move the head a little sideways and move the marker along the bench until relative lateral motion vanishes. Read its coordinate xm​; the estimate is v=xm​<0. Deliberately place the marker nearer and farther to check that relative motion reverses on opposite sides of the match. This follows Orhan Aytür's lens laboratory, which uses a pencil to locate a virtual image. [ref].
Keep target and optical lens fixed, use one eye and the central image detail, and ensure the marker itself is not viewed through the optical lens. A marker blocked by the target, or a head movement that loses the bundle through the aperture, invalidates that trial. Repeat the match from both directions and record its depth range. This measures apparent depth; comparing apparent sizes at different depths does not directly measure transverse magnification. Near u=f, apparent depth becomes very large and the match is poorly constrained. A failed screen search alone therefore needs the distance check and the viewing test.

The surface must be sufficiently smooth on the scale of the wavelength for this model to describe its reflected beam; a visibly flat surface can still scatter light if its microscopic roughness is appreciable. The displayed formula uses unit vectors i,n,r and the dot product. It preserves the component parallel to the mirror and reverses the normal component. For a mirror along y=0, take n=(0,1) and i=(3/5,−4/5). Then i⋅n=−4/5 and r=(3/5,4/5): both directions have vector norm one, and both make an angle arccos(4/5)≈36.87∘ with the relevant normal direction. Replacing n by −n leaves the result unchanged.

The light remains above the mirror; its apparent origin lies below it. A curved mirror changes its normal vector from point to point and can instead make reflected light rays converge. Laser

A laser generates amplified light through stimulated emission. Its name abbreviates “light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation”. Lasers supply the intense beams used in optical tweezers; optical coherence also makes them useful for wave interference measurements. [ref].
In the usual material picture, a gain medium stores energy supplied by pumping, for example by incident light or an electric current. Stimulated emission transfers that stored energy to a selected optical normal mode, while competing photon absorption removes light. Producing net optical gain requires a suitable population distribution, such as population inversion in the simple model below.
A familiar laser oscillator uses mirrors to return light through the gain medium. This optical feedback favours resonant normal modes; a partly transmitting mirror lets useful power escape. Feedback and mode selection have different implementations, including ring arrangements: every laser need not resemble the same two-mirror device. The laser threshold example treats just that device. [ref] [ref].
The useful combination is concentrated power and controlled optical normal modes. It gives optical tweezers a localized source of force and wave interference measurements a source with useful optical coherence. A laser can nevertheless emit several frequencies; “laser” alone does not guarantee a single frequency. [ref].
An original experimental landmark is T. H. Maiman's 1960 report of stimulated optical radiation from optically pumped ruby at about 694.3nm. His paper describes both the pumping path and the observed emission, connecting stored material energy with amplified light. [ref].

Stimulated emission

Laser OurBigBook.com
Stimulated emission is emission induced by incident light, in contrast with the unprompted decay in spontaneous emission. It supplies the amplification mechanism of a laser. [ref].
For an emitter with upper and lower energy values E2​>E1​, the resonant photon has frequency ν satisfying
ΔE=E2​−E1​=hν,
(38)
where h is the Planck constant. In the elementary photon picture, an incident photon stimulates an emitter in the upper quantum state to emit an additional photon into the same optical normal mode, with the same frequency, propagation direction and photon polarization. The emitter supplies the extra energy; the stimulating photon is not consumed. This builds the existing field and its optical coherence. An emitter in the lower quantum state can instead undergo photon absorption, so stimulated emission alone does not establish net optical gain.
For example, a 2.0eV gap corresponds to ν≈4.8360×1014Hz and a vacuum wavelength of about 620nm. One ideal stimulated emission event converts one incoming photon into two outgoing photons in the selected optical normal mode, adding 2.0eV of light energy while lowering the emitter's energy by that amount.

A population inversion puts more emitters in the upper than in the lower quantum state of a transition in the nondegenerate two-level model. Let N2​,N1​ be their number densities. Equal stimulated-transition strengths make the emission rate proportional to N2​ and the competing photon absorption rate proportional to N1​, so net optical gain is proportional to N2​−N1​. For N2​=6×1020m−3 and N1​=4×1020m−3, the difference is positive; swapping them makes the medium absorb. Equal populations give zero net stimulated contribution. With degenerate levels, the relevant comparison uses populations per statistical weight of an atomic level, rather than simply N2​>N1​.
Why pump through extra levels? Ordinary steady resonant pumping of a nondegenerate two-level system drives both photon absorption and stimulated emission. With equal induced rate W and upper-state decay rate Γ, its elementary population equation is
N˙2​=W(N1​−N2​)−ΓN2​,N1​N2​​=W+ΓW​≤1
(39)
at a stationary population. Increasing this pump saturates towards N2​=N1​; it cannot sustain population inversion in this model. This is a steady rate-equation conclusion, not a universal prohibition on all driven two-level dynamics or all possible laser gain mechanisms. [ref].
In a familiar three-level path, pumping excites a higher level which relaxes into the upper lasing level; the lower lasing level is the ground state, so substantial ground-state depletion is needed. A four-level path also provides rapid emptying of the lower lasing level into a separate ground state. Suitable lifetimes then allow accumulation above and depletion below the lasing transition. Pumping still supplies the energy: extra levels provide a route to population inversion, not free energy. [ref].

Optical tweezers hold and move a small particle using the force exerted by a tightly focused beam of light, usually from a laser. They can position transparent beads in a liquid and manipulate suitable biological cells. Attaching a molecule to a trapped bead turns the bead into a handle: a measured bead displacement, together with a calibrated spring constant, reveals the force exerted on the attachment. This makes microscopic manipulation and measurement possible without a mechanical tool touching the bead. Living biological cells were manipulated with infrared beams by Ashkin, Dziedzic and Yamane in 1987; Svoboda and Block used trapped beads to measure forces from individual molecules in 1994. Why can light pull a bead towards a focus? Light carries momentum. A transparent bead with a higher refractive index than the surrounding liquid bends transmitted light rays by refraction, changing their momentum; conservation of momentum requires an opposite transfer to the bead. In the geometrical optics picture, unequal illumination of a displaced bead produces a net restoring force towards the brighter region. For a particle much smaller than the wavelength, a physical optics description replaces that ray picture. The detailed force depends on particle size, refractive index, beam shape and wavelength; the qualitative attraction does not supply a universal formula for every particle.
The optical gradient force draws a suitable transparent bead towards high illumination, while the optical scattering force generally pushes along beam propagation. A stable three-dimensional optical trap needs a balance with a restoring force in each direction: transverse confinement alone does not ensure axial confinement. Strong focusing can make the backward axial gradient contribution large enough to balance the forward scattering contribution, with the equilibrium displaced from the focus. Higher refractive index alone is insufficient; absorbing particles, different index contrasts and different beam geometries can behave differently. [ref].
Historically, Ashkin's 1970 experiments accelerated and trapped particles using radiation pressure. The 1986 paper by Ashkin, Dziedzic, Bjorkholm and Chu demonstrated the single-beam gradient optical trap for transparent particles. These are distinct steps: the earlier work established optical manipulation, and the later work supplied the tightly focused single-beam arrangement. [ref] [ref].
Near a stable equilibrium, a harmonic optical trap behaves like a spring; thermal calibration of an optical trap uses its Brownian motion to determine the effective spring constant. The later passage through a translating optical trap sections instead consider a moving localized potential energy, which need not remain harmonic throughout a passage.

⟨x⟩=0,σ2=Var(x)=⟨x2⟩=kkB​T​.
(45)
At the same temperature, quadrupling the spring constant divides the position variance by four and the standard deviation by two. The Boltzmann factor gives the complete equilibrium probability density function, a Gaussian distribution:
p(x)=2πkB​Tk​​exp(−2kB​Tkx2​),−∞<x<∞.
(46)
The prefactor makes ∫−∞∞​p(x)dx=1; its second moment is ∫−∞∞​x2p(x)dx=kB​T/k. The probability density function has units of inverse length, and its area gives probability. This density is exact for the ideal quadratic model. In a finite optical trap it approximates the occupied well when thermal excursions remain within the harmonic region and escape is negligible during observation. Driven motion, appreciable nonconservative forces or laser heating need not give this equilibrium density.
Here ℓ=kB​T/k0​​, q=x/ℓ and κ=k/k0​. The plotted density per unit q is pq​(q)=ℓp(ℓq)=κ/(2π)​e−κq2/2. Each curve has total area one; their dimensionless standard deviations are 1, 1/2​ and 1/2. The curves are exact model densities, not noisy experimental data.
Brownian motion becomes a measuring tool: a calibrated position measurement supplies σ2=⟨(x−⟨x⟩)2⟩, and the known temperature supplies k=kB​T/σ2. Once k is known, a slowly applied constant external force f shifts the mean by ⟨x⟩=f/k, so f=k⟨x⟩ in the same harmonic range. Fluctuations therefore calibrate the conversion from displacement to force. Svoboda and Block used this equipartition theorem method when calibrating their bead traps. [ref].
For the example stiffness 0.01pN/nm and T=300K, kB​T≈4.142pNnm and σ≈20.35nm. Using a variance measured in uncalibrated detector units would not determine that physical stiffness. Measurement noise, finite exposure time, drift and insufficient sampling of the correlated Brownian motion can bias the estimate; record positions over many optical trap relaxation times and account for the detector response. The deterministic relaxation curve above describes relaxation without thermal forcing; an individual thermal trajectory continues to fluctuate.

Coronagraph

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Optics OurBigBook.com
A coronagraph is an optical instrument that suppresses a bright source's light before detection while transmitting some light from nearby directions. Its purpose is to reveal faint structure buried in the bright source's point spread function, as in exoplanet direct imaging. A Lyot coronagraph combines a coronagraphic focal plane mask with a Lyot stop in a reimaged optical pupil; blocking the central image alone does not remove its diffraction rings. [ref].
The original motivation was the solar corona: hiding the bright photosphere would allow longer, repeated observations of faint surrounding light. In his 1930 paper, Lyot explained that short total eclipses restricted observing time and prevented some long exposures for spectral lines. The attraction is an instrument that makes the faint neighborhood accessible on demand. [ref]. The Sun is an extended source; the point-source calculation below illustrates imaging of an unresolved star and is not a quantitative model of the solar corona.

Lyot coronagraph

Words: 940 Articles: 4
Coronagraph OurBigBook.com
A classical Lyot coronagraph first forms an image of a bright source on the optical axis. A coronagraphic focal plane mask hides its core. Relay optics then form an image of the entrance pupil, where a Lyot stop blocks the outer rim and, when needed, borders around internal obstructions. Finally an optical camera forms the science image. The focal plane sorts incoming directions into image positions; the optical pupil sorts contributions across the aperture. This change of plane makes it possible to reject additional stellar light that survives the first mask. [ref].

Coronagraphic focal plane mask

Words: 59
Lyot coronagraph OurBigBook.com
A coronagraphic focal plane mask modifies the wave amplitude or wave phase in an intermediate focal plane. Here it is a perfectly opaque circular disk centered on the bright source. A finite aperture produces an extended point spread function, so a finite disk blocks only part of the stellar light. Its sharp edge also changes the transmitted field and hence the later diffraction pattern. The exact model below makes both effects visible.

Lyot stop

Words: 65
Lyot coronagraph OurBigBook.com
A Lyot stop is a mask in the reimaged optical pupil after a coronagraphic focal plane mask. For an unobstructed circular entrance pupil, it usually transmits a smaller concentric disk. In a classical Lyot coronagraph, much of the residual stellar field lies near the optical pupil boundary; the Lyot stop rejects that field before the final image is formed. It also rejects useful off-axis light, so choosing its opening involves a coronagraph throughput tradeoff. [ref].

Fourier model of a Lyot coronagraph

Lyot coronagraph OurBigBook.com
Consider an ideal coherent monochromatic wave from an unresolved source on the optical axis, a uniform circular entrance pupil of diameter D, and ideal relay optics without wavefront errors. In the scalar Fraunhofer diffraction approximation, a Fourier transform carries the pupil's complex amplitude into the image plane. Choose dimensionless pupil coordinates x in units of D and angular coordinates u=Dθ/λ, where λ is the wavelength. Define
P(x)={1,0,​∣x∣≤1/2,∣x∣>1/2,​A=FP,(FP)(u)=∫R2​P(x)e−2πix⋅ud2x.
(47)
The coronagraphic focal plane mask has transmission M=1−W, with W=1 inside the occulting disk and W=0 outside. Thus the field immediately after the mask is MA. Outside the disk M=1, so the local wave intensity is still ∣A∣2: hiding the core has left those rings intact. Reimaging an unlimited pupil gives
EL​=F−1(MA)=P−P∗F−1W,Afinal​=F(LEL​),Ifinal​=∣Afinal​∣2,
(48)
where ∗ is convolution, L is the Lyot stop transmission, and the proportionality constant in the irradiance is omitted. Coordinate reversals from physical relay optics are absorbed into the coordinate choice. These equations use wave amplitudes throughout propagation; applying a Fourier transform to wave intensity would give a different and incorrect model. This is the pupil/image calculation described by Sivaramakrishnan et al.; the circular disk and numerical choices below are our illustrative specialization. [ref].
The subtraction explains the beauty of the arrangement: in much of the interior, the original pupil field and the convolution term nearly cancel. Near a boundary, that cancellation is incomplete. The Lyot stop can therefore block a region containing disproportionately much unwanted light. A hard-edged coronagraphic focal plane mask has a transform with extended tails, so the interior need not be perfectly dark. With an unlimited relay, L=1 gives Afinal​=MA exactly: no further ring suppression occurs. A stop covering the full original optical pupil instead uses L=P and already clips field outside the optical pupil; an undersized Lyot stop clips more of the remaining rim.
The toy uses a coronagraphic focal plane mask of angular radius 3λ/D and a Lyot stop of diameter 0.8D. The discrete Fourier transform grid has 1024×1024 samples, with 128 across D and angular sampling 0.125λ/D; it approximates the continuous equations on a finite periodic domain. The plot averages wave intensity in annuli of width 0.25λ/D. Over the annulus 4≤∣u∣≤10, the mean wave intensity divided by the direct stellar peak is approximately 1.40×10−4 without a coronagraph, the same with only the focal mask and an unlimited relay, 4.44×10−5 with the mask and full pupil, and 1.66×10−6 with the mask and 0.8D Lyot stop. Thus the undersized opening reduces this particular annular mean about 27-fold relative to the full-pupil comparison. It does not suppress every direction by that factor, and these values do not predict a real instrument's detection limit.
The ideal toy excludes a central obstruction, support vanes, scattering of light, wavefront errors, atmospheric effects, a spread of wavelengths, pointing drift and detector noise. It also contains only the star: no simulated planet or solar corona. For a far off-axis source whose image misses the coronagraphic focal plane mask, the continuous geometric coronagraph throughput of the 0.8D opening tends to 0.82=0.64 relative to the full disk. Rejecting stellar light therefore costs some desired light as well. Enlarging the coronagraphic focal plane mask narrows the characteristic scale of its pupil-plane transform by the scaling property of the Fourier transform, but also hides a larger neighborhood of the source.

For a specified photodetector measurement, coronagraph throughput T(θ) is the fraction of a source's light transmitted into that measurement at angular separation θ from the blocked source, relative to a stated reference configuration. Total transmitted power and power inside a small image opening can give different fractions; one must specify which is used. Throughput usually depends on wavelength and separation. A lower stellar residual is useful only in relation to the retained companion signal and noise. Guyon's worked designs plot transmitted off-axis light against separation to expose that tradeoff. [ref].

It requires a criterion, such as a chosen fraction of the far off-axis coronagraph throughput, and is often expressed in units of λ/D. It is not automatically the coronagraphic focal plane mask radius or a guarantee of detection. Small separations make useful source transmission and accurate control of wavefront errors particularly demanding. [ref].

It can remove light from a beam without true absorption, or add light from other directions. Wavelength and particle-size dependence make Rayleigh scattering and aerosol scattering useful probes of planetary atmospheres.

Aperture

Words: 595 Articles: 3
Optics OurBigBook.com
An aperture is an opening that admits light into or through an optical instrument. Its shape and size select the transmitted light rays; an aperture alone does not bend them as an optical lens does. The aperture stop is the opening that most restricts the bundle from an on-axis object point. The entrance pupil is the image of that aperture stop formed by the preceding optical lens elements, viewed from the object side. Consequently the effective collecting diameter D is the entrance pupil diameter, which can differ from the physical hole's diameter. For example, preceding optical lens elements that enlarge a 10mm aperture stop by a factor of two give D=20mm; measuring the physical hole alone would misidentify the focal ratio. [ref].
For an unobscured circular entrance pupil under a uniform beam normal to its plane, the collecting area and admitted radiant flux are
A=4πD2​,Φadmitted​=Epupil​A,
(49)
where Epupil​ is incident irradiance. Doubling D quadruples admitted radiant flux. Obstructions, nonuniform illumination and losses after the entrance pupil require the actual illuminated area and transmission to be included. The same D also sets an angular diffraction-limited resolution scale λ/D at wavelength λ. Collection and diffraction therefore answer different questions from field of view: an aperture selects the bundle from each object point, while the receiving plane's extent helps select which object directions appear in the image.
NASA/JPL's published pinhole demonstration uses two white cards, foil taped over a window in one card, and a small hole pierced in the foil. Sunlight passes through the hole onto the second card; the projected image is viewed on that card. The activity describes a larger image when the card separation increases, improved visibility when the receiving card is shaded, and a separate image from each of several holes. These are qualitative observations of image formation, rather than calibrated measurements of radiant flux or diffraction. [ref].
A proposed quantitative extension replaces sunlight by a steadily illuminated asymmetric target and puts the foil and a translucent receiving screen in a dark box. Record target distance u, hole-to-screen distance b, hole diameter d, image height, orientation and edge blur. Measure screen brightness with a fixed photodetector, or record the screen with an optical camera whose integration time and gain stay fixed. Exchange centred foils of measured d at fixed u,b; then vary b with the same foil. Geometrical optics predicts an inverted image with transverse magnification m=−b/u and a point's geometric blur diameter d(1+b/u). Thus a larger hole admits more radiant flux without changing the central image scale, whereas increasing b enlarges the image. These are predictions to test, not reported data. Keep target illumination and detector position fixed, subtract a hole-covered dark reading, repeat the original foil to check drift, and avoid clipping the detector response. Foil thickness and ragged edges can block oblique light rays; at sufficiently small d, diffraction invalidates the claim that ever smaller holes always sharpen the image. A lensless optical camera has no optical lens focal length: b is a propagation distance, not that focal length.

Infrared

Words: 959
Optics OurBigBook.com
Infrared is electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than the red end of ordinarily visible light. A useful named convention is the CIE range 780nm to 1mm; the approximate visible range 400–700nm used in some teaching texts puts the boundary nearer 700nm. [ref]. Neither number is a sharp physical cutoff of human vision. The CIE divisions IR-A, IR-B and IR-C are respectively 0.78–1.4μm, 1.4–3μm and 3–1000μm; the boundaries of near-, middle- and far-infrared vary between applications. [ref].
Use vacuum wavelength λ when comparing these ranges. With frequency ν, speed of light c, Planck constant h and photon energy E,
ν=λc​,E=hν=λhc​.
(50)
Thus the CIE infrared interval corresponds approximately to 3.00×1011–3.84×1014Hz and 1.99×10−22–2.55×10−19J per photon, with the smaller energy at the longer wavelength. A 940nm infrared photon has E≃2.11×10−19J, whereas a 254nm ultraviolet photon has E≃7.82×10−19J. These are calculations from hc/λ, not measurements of a particular source. A television remote is a familiar approximately 940nm source; its information is carried by variations in the emitted radiant flux. [ref].
Detection and visual perception answer different questions. A photodetector can respond to infrared even when an observer perceives no light; a thermometer detects an increase in temperature after photon absorption. Conversely, a small readout can reflect a small spectral responsivity, rather than absence of incident electromagnetic radiation. Images made from infrared readouts use display colors chosen by the imaging system; those colors are not the colors of the incoming infrared.
The important microscopic mechanisms also differ. In infrared spectroscopy, photon absorption often increases the energy of a normal mode in which chemical bonds stretch or bend. The corresponding optical spectrum helps distinguish molecules by their motions. For the usual electric dipole mechanism, the motion must change the electric dipole moment; matching the frequency alone is not sufficient. [ref]. Electronic processes can also emit or absorb infrared, so it is not exclusively radiation from molecular motion. [ref]; [ref].
Infrared is especially useful for observing thermal radiation from objects near everyday temperatures. For an ideal 300K blackbody, Wien's displacement law gives a wavelength peak near 9.66μm. A thermal camera's readout nevertheless depends on emissivity, reflected surroundings and transmission along the path, as well as temperature. [ref]. A source emitting infrared need not be hot: an infrared remote is useful precisely because a photodetector can distinguish its signal from a background. Visible light and ultraviolet can also cause heating when absorbed; “infrared” names a wavelength range, not a unique form of heat.
Herschel's 1800 discovery made the distinction between sight and detection experimentally concrete. His report describes a optical prism spreading sunlight across a white, ruled receiving surface, with three thermometers at different positions near the end of the visible optical spectrum. He observed heating beyond the red edge where no visible color appeared. The result established that sunlight contained invisible radiation less strongly refracted by that optical prism than the visible red; it did not measure a photon energy or establish today's infrared boundaries. [ref]; [ref].
A documented modern version by Caltech/IPAC uses a glass optical prism, white paper in a shaded box and three blackened liquid-filled thermometers. Initial readings in shade provide each thermometer's baseline; subsequent readings compare blue, yellow and just beyond red after the bulbs have had time to warm. The measured quantity is the rise in temperature, not a “temperature of a color”. The lesson reports the expected largest rise beyond visible red and specifically discusses matching the bulb coatings and thermometer calibration. Clouds and changes in the projected optical spectrum affect the comparison. [ref].
For a stronger modern interpretation, an additional shaded thermometer would monitor ambient drift, exchanging bulbs between positions would test differences between thermometers, and blocking the incident beam would distinguish beam-dependent heating from warmed supports or air. These are suggested controls, not claims about Herschel's historical procedure. Thermal conduction through the mounting and convection can change the readout. A broad bulb also samples a range of wavelengths; the optical prism's transmission and optical dispersion, the bulb's absorption and heat loss all affect the position of the largest rise. In particular, the result does not show that an infrared photon carries more energy than a visible photon.
A simple analytical illustration makes those limitations explicit. Let θ=T−Tamb​ be the bulb's excess temperature, C its heat capacity, G its effective heat-loss coefficient in WK−1, and Pabs​ the absorbed power. Assume one uniform bulb temperature, constant ambient temperature, constant C,G, and losses linear in θ. Then
Cdtdθ​=Pabs​−Gθ,θ(t)=GPabs​​(1−e−t/τ),τ=GC​,
(51)
for a beam switched on at t=0 with θ(0)=0. After switching the beam off at t=ts​, θ(t)=θ(ts​)e−(t−ts​)/τ. The exponential function follows by solving this linear differential equation. The steady excess temperature measures Pabs​/G; it is not a direct measurement of the optical spectrum. With illustrative C=0.020JK−1 and G=0.0010WK−1, τ=20s. Absorbed powers of 1.0 and 0.5mW give steady rises of 1.0 and 0.5K, regardless of which wavelengths supplied that absorbed power.
The upper schematic represents the logic of the optical prism experiment; its light ray positions are not a calibrated wavelength scale. The lower curves use the illustrative heat-balance model, with the beam blocked at 60s; they are not historical or modern measured data. The beauty of the experiment is that a simple change of detector extends observation beyond what the eye can perceive.

Ultraviolet

Words: 925
Optics OurBigBook.com
Ultraviolet is electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than the violet end of ordinarily visible light. The CIE convention uses 100–400nm, subdivided into UV-A at 315–400nm, UV-B at 280–315nm and UV-C at 100–280nm. These divisions name intervals; they do not mark universal changes in every material's response. The boundary with visible light is not sharp, and other fields use near-, far-, vacuum- and extreme-ultraviolet divisions. [ref]. For example, NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory observes extreme-ultraviolet bands below 100nm; the CIE interval is therefore not the full extent of astronomical ultraviolet usage. [ref].
The CIE ultraviolet interval corresponds to frequencies about 7.49×1014–3.00×1015Hz and photon energies 4.97×10−19–1.99×10−18J, using vacuum wavelength and E=hc/λ with Planck constant h and speed of light c. Shorter wavelength means larger energy per photon; larger irradiance means more incident power per area. These are different comparisons. At the same incident power, a 254nm ultraviolet beam has fewer photons per second than a 940nm infrared beam, even though each ultraviolet photon has more energy.
A common ultraviolet mechanism is photon absorption promoting an Electron from a ground state to an excited state of a chemical atom or molecule. By contrast, many infrared absorption bands involve stretching or bending chemical bonds. For either mechanism, both the energy difference and the coupling to the incident electromagnetic field matter. One concrete example is the 217nm absorption discussed for butadiene: an Electron moves between molecular orbitals, and the position of the absorption reveals their energy separation. Ultraviolet absorption can therefore probe molecular orbitals, while infrared spectroscopy probes many molecular motions. [ref].
Subsequent chemical reactions depend on the absorbing chemical substance and its environment; the label ultraviolet alone does not predict a reaction rate. At sufficiently short wavelength, a photon can cause photoionization if its energy exceeds the relevant ionization energy. There is no single wavelength that separates all ionizing from all nonionizing behavior for every chemical substance. Likewise, eventual heating after photon absorption is possible in both ultraviolet and infrared. The distinction is useful because different optical spectra expose different processes, not because the two ranges obey different laws of electromagnetism.
Ritter's 1801 observation used a chemical readout rather than a thermometer. In Caltech/IPAC's account, sunlight passed through a glass optical prism and silver chloride was placed in different parts of the optical spectrum. Darkening was weak toward red, stronger toward violet, and pronounced beyond the visible violet edge. The measured evidence was a change in the chemical substance's appearance at a spatial location with no visible color, establishing radiation beyond the eye's ordinary range. It was not a calibrated measurement of a universal ultraviolet optical spectrum. [ref].
A controlled modern interpretation of such a chemical test would compare equal exposure durations and matched fresh samples, keep an unexposed sample in darkness, monitor temperature, and distinguish scattered visible light from the intended short-wavelength beam with characterized filtering. These are proposed controls, not an assertion that Ritter performed them. Unequal sample preparation or heating can change a reaction rate. The optical prism, terrestrial atmosphere and sample response restrict which wavelengths the test detects. Darkening is a detector-weighted response, so its spatial maximum is not automatically the maximum of incoming radiant flux or of photon energy.
Thomas Larason and Jeanne Houston's NIST report documents a quantitative ultraviolet detector comparison. An argon source feeds a double-diffraction grating spectrometer; a shutter and mirrors deliver the selected band to a working-standard or test photodiode, successively at the same position. A beam splitter supplies a monitor photodiode. Amplifiers and voltmeters record detector and monitor simultaneously; shutter-closed readings provide dark baselines. The 200–500nm scan, typically with 4nm bandpass, measures spectral responsivity. Monitor normalization suppresses source drift; known spectral lines calibrate wavelength. The report assesses temperature effects and unwanted light outside the band, weighted by detector response. The latter need not cancel between different spectral responsivities. [ref].
This determines electrical response without visual perception. Bandpass and spatial nonuniformity limit the calibration; aging and changed temperature can affect later use. The scan includes visible light and ultraviolet; no response below 200nm follows from it.
For a narrow beam, the idealized substitution calculation is
Rtest​(λ)=Rstd​(λ)Istd​/Mstd​Itest​/Mtest​​.
(52)
Here R is spectral responsivity; I and M are dark-subtracted detector and monitor electric currents. This follows by writing I=RP for each detector and using the monitor to track changes in radiant flux. It assumes linear response, unchanged beam splitting and collection geometry, and a sufficiently narrow band. For an illustrative standard with Rstd​=0.15AW−1, ratios Istd​/Mstd​=2.0 and Itest​/Mtest​=1.6 give Rtest​=0.12AW−1. These invented arithmetic inputs illustrate the method; they are not NIST measurements.
An independent photon-counting model connects spectral responsivity to quantum efficiency. If η(λ) is the number of collected Electrons per incident photon, there is no internal multiplication, and q is the elementary charge, then
N˙=hcPλ​,I=qηN˙,R(λ)=PI​=η(λ)hcqλ​.
(53)
At illustrative constant η=0.60 and P=1μW, this gives about 0.123μA at 254nm and 0.455μA at 940nm. The ultraviolet readout is smaller in this model because there are fewer incident photons, not because their individual energies are smaller. Real quantum efficiency depends on wavelength, windows, absorption and carrier collection; a detector's band gap and construction determine its usable range. Constant η across these two wavelengths is an analytical comparison, not a claimed specification of a real photodiode.
The curve is the calculated relation E=hc/λ, and the shaded ranges use the stated CIE conventions. The lower diagram abstracts the detector comparison rather than reproducing an instrument drawing. Together with the infrared heat-balance illustration, it shows why a calibrated detector response, rather than what looks bright to an observer, is the bridge between invisible radiation and a quantitative measurement.

A fundamental Gaussian beam is an ideal beam of light whose transverse wave amplitude has a Gaussian function profile. Here consider a circularly symmetric beam in vacuum, with propagation along z, two transverse coordinates x,y, and radius r=x2+y2​ from the optical axis. With the beam waist at z=0, total power P>0, and vacuum wavelength λ, its time-averaged light intensity, meaning irradiance in Wm−2, is
I(r,z)=πw(z)22P​exp(−w(z)22r2​),w(z)=w0​1+(zR​z​)2​,zR​=λπw02​​.
(54)
Here w0​ is the minimum beam radius, and zR​ is the Rayleigh range. Far from the beam waist, w(z)∼θ∣z∣ with beam divergence half-angle θ=λ/(πw0​). These are the fundamental circular Gaussian beam laws within the scalar paraxial approximation, appropriate when w0​≫λ and the beam divergence is small. The underlying envelope solves the parabolic wave equation exactly; this does not make it an exact vector solution of Maxwell equations. [ref].
The radius convention matters. Writing U for the complex wave amplitude envelope, the same w(z) is the wave amplitude 1/e radius and the light intensity 1/e2 radius:
∣U(0,z)∣∣U(r,z)∣​=e−r2/w(z)2,I(0,z)I(r,z)​=e−2r2/w(z)2.
(55)
At r=w(z) these ratios are e−1≈0.367879 and e−2≈0.135335, respectively. The light intensity 1/e radius is instead w(z)/2​. None of these radii is a sharp edge: the ideal Gaussian function has nonzero tails at every finite radius. Kogelnik and Li explicitly use the wave amplitude 1/e radius in their fundamental-mode treatment. [ref].
For a numerical example, take vacuum wavelength λ=632.8nm and beam waist radius w0​=0.500mm. Substitution gives Rayleigh range zR​≈1.24114754m and far-field beam divergence half-angle θ≈0.402852992mrad. At z=zR​, the beam radius is w=2​w0​≈0.707107mm and the on-axis irradiance is half its waist value. At the same wavelength, halving the beam waist radius to 0.250mm quarters the Rayleigh range to 0.310286885m and doubles the beam divergence half-angle to 0.805705984mrad. At fixed power, that smaller beam waist also quadruples the peak irradiance.
The contours in the left panel are r=±w(z) in a plane through the optical axis; they mark an light intensity level, not an outer boundary. The right panel compares the exact model radii with the far-field asymptotes w=θz. The horizontal and vertical axes use different length units, so the drawn slopes are not physical angles.
The normalization expresses conserved power during free propagation. In transverse polar coordinates, an annulus has area 2πrdr, so
∫R2​Idxdy=2π∫0∞​I(r,z)rdr=P,PP(r<a)​=1−e−2a2/w(z)2.

A proof outline is the substitution s=2r2/w(z)2 in this integral. Spreading reduces peak irradiance as w−2 while increasing transverse area as w2, leaving power unchanged. In particular, the disk of radius w(z) contains 1−e−2≈0.8646647168, or 86.4665%, of the total power; the local light intensity at its rim is only 13.5335% of the on-axis light intensity. These are different quantities.
The left panel compares normalized wave amplitude magnitude and irradiance; the right panel integrates the transverse area to show enclosed power. For an ideal absorbing circular aperture of radius a centered on the optical axis, the same fraction gives the power passing the aperture at that plane. An aperture of radius w clips about 13.5335% of the incident power; radius 2w clips only e−8≈0.000335463, or 0.0335463%. After clipping, extra diffraction means the transmitted field no longer obeys the unmodified ideal Gaussian beam law. Every finite aperture cuts some ideal tail. Kogelnik and Li distinguish their large-aperture beam analysis from their finite-aperture diffraction analysis. [ref].
The useful tradeoff is that a small bright spot cannot remain narrow indefinitely. An optical lens can create a smaller beam waist, but diffraction then makes the beam spread faster. The particularly simple relation w0​θ=λ/π ties localization directly to beam divergence. A proof outline for the propagation law starts with U(x,y,0)=U0​e−(x2+y2)/w02​. The parabolic wave equation separates into two transverse factors, and a Gaussian integral in each coordinate gives
U(x,y,z)=q(z)U0​​exp(−w02​q(z)x2+y2​),q(z)=1+izR​z​,k=λ2π​.

Here q is dimensionless and k is the wavenumber; the carrier convention is ei(kz−ωt), with angular frequency ω. Taking the squared complex modulus gives the stated w(z) and its w−2 light intensity scaling. Each transverse factor contributes q−1/2, explaining the q−1 prefactor here and the different prefactor in the preserved Gaussian beam with one transverse coordinate.
Historically, Gaussian beam theory developed alongside early laser resonator theory and lens-guided transmission. In their 1966 review, Kogelnik and Li credit Boyd and Gordon, and Goubau and Schwering, with early beam treatments; they summarize earlier work rather than claim the whole construction as a new discovery. Their paper brings beam propagation, focusing and finite-aperture diffraction into a common practical account. [ref].

The beam waist is the narrowest cross-section of a freely propagating Gaussian beam. Its radius w0​ uses the wave amplitude 1/e, or light intensity 1/e2, convention; its diameter is 2w0​. Specifying a “spot size” without saying radius or diameter can introduce a factor-of-two error. Within the scalar paraxial approximation, the wavefront at the beam waist is planar. The minimum radius sets both the Rayleigh range and the far-field beam divergence.

Gaussian beam OurBigBook.com
The Rayleigh range of a fundamental Gaussian beam in vacuum is the positive axial distance from the beam waist at which its radius grows from w0​ to 2​w0​. Thus its contour area doubles and its peak irradiance halves. Within ∣z∣≤zR​, the radius stays at most 2​w0​; for ∣z∣≫zR​, beam divergence dominates. At fixed vacuum wavelength, the Rayleigh range scales quadratically with the beam waist radius. The formula here uses the vacuum wavelength, not an unlabelled wavelength in a material.

Wavefront

Words: 2k Articles: 6
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
A wavefront connects points with the same wave phase at one specified time. It is a surface, rather than the trajectory of a particular piece of light. For a scalar monochromatic wave written as u(r,t)=A(r)cosΦ(r,t), a wavefront is a connected level set of the phase function Φ; different surfaces can share the same wave phase modulo 2π. A plane wave has planar wavefronts. An outward wave from an ideal point source in a uniform medium has spheres as wavefronts, while an optical lens can turn nearly planar wavefronts into converging ones. The wavefront describes wave phase, not wave amplitude: drawing it does not say how bright the beam is. [ref]
The relation to light rays becomes precise in a stationary medium with isotropy, negligible loss and a real positive scalar refractive index n(r,ω). In the geometrical optics limit, spatial changes in the refractive index and wave amplitude are slow on the local wavelength scale. For a single smooth propagation branch, write
Φ(r,t)=k0​S(r,ω)−ωt+ϕ0​,k0​=cω​,∣∇S∣2=n2.
(60)
Here ω>0 is the angular frequency, c is the vacuum speed of light, S has units of length, and the last relation is the optical eikonal equation. The local wavevector is k=∇Φ=k0​∇S. Its direction is normal to a smooth wavefront, since a gradient is normal to its level sets. A forward light ray has unit tangent vector dr/ds=∇S/n, so it follows this normal under the stated assumptions. Along that light ray, dS/ds=∇S⋅(dr/ds)=n: the change in S is the optical path length. This is the short geometric argument linking wavefronts, light rays and optical path length. [ref]
The diagram shows incident and transmitted branches separately, with the reflected branch omitted. Its stipulated refractive indices are n1​=1 and n2​=3/2, and its incident angle is 30∘ to the interface normal. At a stationary interface, the frequency and tangential wavevector agree on the two sides: Snell's law gives sinθ2​=1/3, hence θ2​≈19.4712∘. The wavefronts turn while their normal spacing decreases from λ0​ to 2λ0​/3, where λ0​ is the vacuum wavelength. More explicitly, with x normal to the interface and y tangential, take S1​=3​x/2+y/2 for x<0 and S2​=2​x+y/2 for x>0. These functions agree at x=0; the drawn wavefronts are Sj​=mλ0​ at t=0 with ϕ0​=0. This is an exact piecewise plane wave phase construction for the stipulated transparent media, not measured material data. [ref]
The normal-to-wavefront rule requires its assumptions. In a medium with anisotropy, the wavevector remains normal to a smooth wavefront, but the group velocity and energy flux need not follow it. [ref] Near a wave caustic, where multiple light rays meet, one smooth phase function may no longer describe the field; diffraction and the full wave amplitude matter. A wavefront is also not generally a surface of equal pulse arrival time. In a medium with optical dispersion, a monochromatic wave phase moves with the phase velocity, while a sufficiently narrow wave packet follows the group velocity. Even identical optical path lengths at one frequency can give different group delays. The usual equal-travel-time picture needs a common launch reference and a nondispersive ray model; an arbitrary broadband disturbance has no single monochromatic wavefront.[ref]
