An optical path length measures how much propagation wave phase a path accumulates, expressed as the distance that would accumulate the same wave phase in vacuum. A centimetre in a uniform medium with refractive index 3/2 has optical path length 1.5cm, although its geometric length remains 1cm. This makes optical path length useful whenever two contributions must arrive with matching wave phases, from an optical lens to a Michelson interferometer. [ref]
For a specified path γ at fixed angular frequency ω, the optical path length is the line integral
OPLγ​(ω)=∫γ​n(r,ω)ds,ds=∣dr∣,OPL=∑j​nj​Lj​ for uniform segments.
(61)
Here s is geometric arc length, and n is the phase refractive index, evaluated at the same frequency everywhere. The propagation interpretation assumes a stationary linear medium with isotropy, a real positive scalar refractive index and negligible loss, on a valid geometrical optics branch. The path can curve; at sharp interfaces apply the appropriate matching conditions to each segment. A prescribed curve has a mathematical line integral, but it predicts a propagation wave phase only when it represents the physical branch. [ref] Optical fibers can require a mode wavenumber rather than the bulk refractive index along a guessed light ray. [ref]
Fix the vacuum wavelength λ0​=c/f=2πc/ω, with frequency f=ω/(2π) and vacuum wavenumber k0​=2π/λ0​. In a locally uniform medium the wavelength is λ=λ0​/n, while the frequency stays unchanged at a stationary interface. With the convention Φ=k0​S−ωt+ϕ0​, propagation from a specified starting wave phase contributes
ϕprop​=k0​OPL,δ=δref​+k0​(OPL2​−OPL1​)(mod2π).
(62)
The relative reference δref​ includes launch wave phases and any extra wave phase from mirrors, beam splitters or coatings. Thus k0​OPL is a propagation contribution, not an absolute detector wave phase independent of the apparatus. If the reference contributions stay fixed, a change in optical path difference h changes the phase difference by 2πh/λ0​. Using the material wavelength again in this formula would count the refractive index twice. [ref]
A motivating measurement turns invisible optical oscillations into a slowly changing electrical signal. MIT's teaching experiment uses a laser, a beam splitter, two returning mirrors, an amplified photodiode, an oscilloscope and a calibrated mirror actuator driven by a function generator. The returning beams overlap on the photodiode; one channel records detector voltage and another the actuator drive. The measured observable is the changing light intensity, including its maxima and minima, rather than direct timing of an optical cycle. A calibrated displacement per drive voltage and the spacing of the extrema relate geometric motion to the phase difference. The guide infers the laser wavelength from known actuator calibration; conversely, with independently known vacuum wavelength and ambient refractive index, the same relation calibrates mirror motion. These two unknowns cannot both be inferred from fringe spacing alone. [ref]
For a proposed change-of-medium measurement, keep the mirrors fixed and put a transparent cell of internal length L in one arm. Compare its contents at refractive indices na​ and nb​, leaving its windows in place. At normal incidence the two traversals give
ΔOPL=2L(nb​−na​),Δδ=λ0​4πL(nb​−na​)​,N=2πΔδ​=λ0​2L(nb​−na​)​.
(63)
Here N is the signed number of whole interference fringe cycles plus any resolved fractional cycle, counted continuously. A mirror displacement x instead gives ΔOPL=2namb​x; distinguish this double-pass factor from a single pass in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. OpenStax's gas-cell worked example provides the same double-pass reasoning; it is a teaching calculation rather than a published measurement dataset.[ref]
An exact toy calculation makes the sensitivity visible. Stipulate λ0​=600nm, L=10mm and nb​−na​=3/100000=0.00003. Then ΔOPL=600nm and Δδ=2π: a full interference fringe cycle, despite unchanged geometric lengths. For a continuous change nb​−na​=q(3/100000), let 0≤q≤2 and choose the initial detector phase difference to be zero. Equal coherent detected arm contributions of light intensity I0​ predict
4I0​I(q)​=21+cos(2πq)​=cos2(πq).
(64)
The plot is this stipulated model: q=1/2 gives a minimum, q=1 restores a maximum, and the reference level is chosen by adjustment of the apparatus. It contains no measured values or assigned properties of a real gas. The equivalent mirror travel in vacuum is 300nm per cycle. A single endpoint light intensity cannot distinguish q=0 from q=1; the continuous fringe count carries the missing information.
For an interpretable cell measurement, establish the initial phase difference with a small calibrated mirror scan, then track slow changes through successive interference fringes. Measure the dark signal and each arm separately, keep photodiode gain within its linear range, align both beams on the same region and match their linear polarizations. Monitor interferometric visibility and keep arm delays within the useful optical coherence time. Record cell length, contents, pressure and temperature; return to the starting condition to check drift. Changes in window deformation, cell length, external air or mirror position also change optical path length, so a reference cell or an independently monitored mechanical path is needed to isolate the contents' refractive index. These controls are deductions from the model, not a claim that the illustrated apparatus was operated. Loss of fringe count leaves a whole-cycle ambiguity; at an intensity extremum the first derivative with respect to phase difference vanishes, so a scan around phase quadrature is more sensitive to small changes. Broadband illumination, unstable optical coherence, vibration and strong loss can invalidate a simple one-frequency inference.

Interference (wave propagation)

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Wave interference is the reinforcement or cancellation that occurs when overlapping wave amplitudes add by the superposition principle. For two monochromatic waves of the same frequency, mutual optical coherence means that their relative wave phase is stable during the observation. Equal wave phases give constructive interference; a half-cycle phase difference gives the destructive interference intensity minimum. Wave amplitudes add before their squares determine wave intensity. [ref].
Consider two overlapping beams in a homogeneous medium, with the same polarization of an electromagnetic wave and individual local time-averaged light intensities I1​,I2​. Their phase difference δ is measured in radians. In the scalar detection convention, the combined local time-averaged wave intensity is
I=I1​+I2​+2I1​I2​​cosδ.
(66)
The last term records wave interference; adding I1​+I2​ alone misses it. The formula describes irradiance when both fields propagate along the same direction, or when the same detector geometry factor is included in all three intensities. For crossing beams it describes the squared electric field response, proportional to scalar wave intensity; a specified component of the Poynting vector also requires the propagation geometry. The ideal crossing plane waves below make that distinction explicit.
For equal individual light intensities I1​=I2​=I0​>0, the cosine half-angle identity gives
I=2I0​(1+cosδ)=4I0​cos2(δ/2).
(67)
The constructive interference intensity is 4I0​ at δ=0 modulo 2π, and the destructive interference intensity is zero at δ=π modulo 2π. At phase quadrature, δ=π/2, it is 2I0​. With I1​=1 and I2​=0.25 in the same arbitrary wave intensity unit, the maximum is 2.25, the minimum is 0.25, and the phase quadrature value is 1.25: unequal wave amplitudes cannot cancel completely.
Both curves use the same wave intensity unit and a horizontal angle in radians. The dashed levels are the averages over a full phase difference cycle. Equal beams have interferometric visibility one; the unequal example has interferometric visibility 0.8.
A spatially varying phase difference turns the same law into interference fringes. Take two ideal plane electromagnetic waves with common wavelength λ, equal individual light intensities I0​, and propagation directions at angles +θ and −θ from the z axis in the xz plane, with 0<θ<π/2. Both have linear polarization along y, perpendicular to both propagation directions. Choose equal initial wave phases; their wavevectors and phase difference are
k±​=k(±sinθ,0,cosθ),k=λ2π​,ϕ±​=±kxsinθ+kzcosθ−ωt,δ=ϕ+​−ϕ−​=2kxsinθ.
(68)
Here k is the wavenumber and ω the angular frequency. The common z and time terms cancel, so the interference fringes stay at fixed x for every z. Their interference fringe spacing is
Λ=2ksinθ2π​=2sinθλ​,I0​I(x,z)​=4cos2(kxsinθ).
(69)
Set the length unit to λ, so that λ=1, and take θ=30∘=π/6: then Λ=1. The constructive interference intensity bands lie at integer x/λ; the destructive interference intensity bands lie at half-integer x/λ.
The grid covers −3≤x/λ≤3 and 0≤z/λ≤4; both axes are dimensionless lengths in wavelength units. The colour scale is I/I0​ from zero to four, using the same single-beam normalization as the equal-beam curve above. This is an ideal plane wave superposition, with no slits or point sources and no near-field approximation. For these y-polarized plane electromagnetic waves in vacuum, the longitudinal time-averaged Poynting vector obeys ⟨Sz​⟩=Icosθ; the plotted scalar I therefore differs from the irradiance through a plane normal to z by that common factor. This relation follows by adding the magnetic fields as well as the electric fields.
The bright peaks do not create energy. Averaging over one interference fringe spacing, or equivalently over one full phase difference cycle, gives
2π1​∫02π​I(δ)dδ=I1​+I2​,
(70)
because the integral of the cosine is zero, with sine as its antiderivative. Equal beams thus average to 2I0​, despite bright bands at 4I0​. For the crossing-wave geometry, the average longitudinal energy flux is correspondingly 2I0​cosθ. Bright and dark regions redistribute the incoming energy; conservation of energy concerns the full energy flux, rather than the height of one peak.
Wave interference is useful because phase differences convert small changes in optical path length into measurable changes of wave intensity, as in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Its beauty is that the same superposition principle produces both complete cancellation and fourfold brightening; adding more coherent contributions also produces the narrow peaks of a diffraction grating. Feynman's treatment connects this many-source pattern directly to addition of complex amplitudes. [ref].
A short proof outline uses local real fields Ej​(t)=Aj​cos(ωt+ϕj​) with parallel linear polarizations. Write I=C⟨(E1​+E2​)2⟩t​ and Ij​=CAj2​/2 for the same positive conversion factor C. Averaging over many wave periods while the phase difference stays fixed uses ⟨cos2(ωt+ϕj​)⟩t​=1/2 and ⟨cos(ωt+ϕ1​)cos(ωt+ϕ2​)⟩t​=cosδ/2, giving the stated law. Equivalently, add the complex amplitudes and take the squared complex modulus. [ref].
For different fixed linear polarizations in a common transverse plane, the cross term acquires the dot product of their real unit vectors, equal to cosα for relative angle α. Orthogonal linear polarizations remove the cross term in polarization-insensitive scalar detection; different orientations generally only reduce it. A common polarizer can select overlapping components and recover wave interference. Likewise, rapid random variation of the phase difference removes the observed cross term only when the detector's time average has ⟨eiδ(t)⟩t​=0. Slowly varying wave phases can instead move resolved interference fringes, and biased or incompletely sampled wave phases can leave residual contrast. Finite optical coherence therefore depends on the observation time as well as the fields.

An interference fringe is a spatial band of enhanced or reduced wave intensity caused by a spatially varying phase difference. Uniform crossing plane waves produce straight parallel interference fringes; curved wavefronts can give curved bands. The interference fringes mark the relative wave phase, rather than the individual instantaneous wavefronts.

The distance between adjacent bright interference fringes, or between adjacent dark interference fringes, measured along a specified direction. For the symmetric crossing plane waves in wave interference, measured along x, Λ=λ/(2sinθ). Bright-to-dark separation is Λ/2. As θ tends to zero the spacing diverges; at θ=0 the phase difference is spatially constant and there are no periodic bands.

Fraunhofer diffraction is the far-field approximation for diffraction: contributions from an aperture reach a selected observation direction with approximately linear path-dependent wave phases. Adding their complex amplitudes gives a Fourier transform of the field across the aperture. It also describes the appropriate rear focal plane of an ideal optical lens under coherent plane-wave illumination. The diffraction grating examples use this regime. [ref]; [ref].
For a slit of width a, wavelength λ and screen distance L, sufficient conditions near the forward direction are
L≫a,L≫λa2​,λLa2​≪1.
(72)
The last two statements are equivalent: the important comparison is with a2/λ, rather than just with the slit width. For a finite rectangular aperture, check the corresponding condition for both transverse dimensions. The single-slit diffraction calculation treats the transverse cut associated with width a. [ref].
A short explanation is that the distance from slit coordinate x to an observation point at distance R and angle θ is

A narrower aperture requires a larger angle to accumulate the cancelling phase difference, so narrowing the slit widens the beam. This is a useful limit on geometrical optics: confining light more tightly at an opening increases its subsequent angular spread. Optical coherence

Words: 2k Articles: 6
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Optical coherence describes correlations between the wave amplitudes and wave phases of light sampled at different places or times. Its most direct classical test is wave interference: combine two samples of a field and see how much the detected light intensity changes when their relative wave phase is scanned. First-order optical coherence makes this statement quantitative; temporal optical coherence compares delayed samples, while spatial optical coherence compares different positions. These properties are relative to the samples and averaging procedure, rather than a single yes-or-no label for a source. [ref].
A useful surprise is that two copies of a fluctuating source can interfere strongly when they have matched delays: the copies share the fluctuations. Conversely, two individually steady-looking beams need not have correlated wave phases. The ideal diffraction grating calculation requires spatial optical coherence across its illuminated elements; unequal-arm measurements with a Michelson interferometer test temporal optical coherence.

Γ12​(τ)=⟨E1∗​(t)E2​(t+τ)⟩,g12(1)​(τ)=J1​J2​​Γ12​(τ)​,J1​,J2​>0.

The one-position version is g(1)(τ)=⟨E∗(t)E(t+τ)⟩/⟨∣E∣2⟩, so g(1)(0)=1 for every nonzero field covered by this definition; this alone says nothing about its correlation at nonzero delay. [ref].

At a specified delay, magnitude one means E2​(t+τ)=aE1​(t) in mean square for a fixed nonzero complex a: the samples have a reproducible relation in both wave amplitude and wave phase. Magnitude zero means the averaged field cross term vanishes. It need not mean statistical independence. A deterministic phase difference changes the argument of g(1), not its complex modulus; a distorted but fixed wavefront can therefore remain fully coherent. [ref].

The extra wave phase scan must leave I1​,I2​ and the magnitude of the correlation effectively unchanged. For I2​/I1​=1/4, perfectly coherent beams have interferometric visibility 0.8; a measured value 0.4 would imply ∣g(1)∣=0.5 under these assumptions. Orthogonal linear polarizations, background light, unresolved interference fringes or vibrations can reduce measured contrast further. Temporal optical coherence compares a field at one position with a delayed copy. In a Michelson interferometer, unequal round-trip lengths supply this delay. Even a source with rapidly changing wave phase can give high interferometric visibility close to zero delay, because both arms then deliver nearly the same source history. A source narrowed in optical spectrum generally retains correlation over larger delays; a single width does not describe sources with several separated lines. [ref].
For a stationary scalar field, choose the carrier convention e−i2πνt, with frequency ν in cycles per second. Let S(ν)≥0 be its spectral density per unit frequency, with 0<∫S(ν)dν<∞. Its normalized field correlation is the Fourier transform

The optical spectrum weights the rotating contributions; a broad spread of frequencies allows them to cancel at short delays. This is the stationary field correlation–spectrum relation. The relevant spectrum is that of the optical field in the detected mode, rather than the low-frequency fluctuations of a detector's light intensity. [ref].
Here are two stipulated line profiles, each centered at ν0​ with full width at half maximum Δν>0. Write f=ν−ν0​ and use normalized profiles on the whole detuning line:

The detuning approximation treats the narrow line as extending to arbitrarily large positive and negative f; for optical applications require Δν≪ν0​. Changing to angular frequency replaces Δν by Δω/(2π); it must not silently preserve the same numerical constant.
Equal detected single-arm light intensities give interferometric visibility equal to the correlation magnitude. Doubling the Gaussian full width at half maximum from 1 to 2GHz halves every fixed-contrast delay. At τ=0.5ns the model gives Gaussian interferometric visibility approximately 0.410686 at 1GHz and 0.0284471 at 2GHz; the 1GHz Lorentzian gives 0.207880. Michelson interferometer
Words: 452
Temporal optical coherence OurBigBook.com
A Michelson interferometer divides light at a beam splitter, reflects the two arms at mirrors and recombines the returning fields. For vacuum arm lengths ℓ1​,ℓ2​, the delay magnitude is ∣τ∣=2∣ℓ2​−ℓ1​∣/c. At each coarse delay, a small mirror scan produces maxima and minima of the detected light intensity. A photodiode and its electrical readout resolve these changes; the scan should cover several carrier cycles while changing ∣g(1)∣ negligibly. MIT's laboratory guide uses a mirror actuator, photodiode and electrical drive to scan interference fringes and extract interferometric visibility.[ref]
A verified motivating experiment is Shaoul Ezekiel's MIT demonstration of source-spectrum control. A polarizer selects one or several lines from a laser whose adjacent lines have orthogonal linear polarizations. A sampled beam goes to a scanning Fabry–Pérot interferometer to check the optical spectrum; the main beam enters a Michelson interferometer, and a lens projects its interference fringes onto a screen. With one selected line the fringes retain good contrast through the demonstrated delay range. With several lines their contrast falls and returns as the arm length changes. At a fixed delay with poor contrast, selecting one line restores it; at matched arms both selections give good contrast. This control isolates the role of spectral composition rather than simply the arm position. The presentation is a qualitative demonstration, not a calibrated linewidth measurement. [ref].
A deliberately simpler two-line model explains the return of contrast. Take two stationary, mutually uncorrelated monochromatic contributions of equal power at ν0​±δν/2. Their normalized wave-field correlation is
g(1)(τ)=e−i2πν0​τcos(πδντ),V(τ)=∣cos(πδντ)∣
(86)
for equal detected single-arm light intensities. At τ=1/(2δν) the two contributions' interference fringes cancel on averaging; at τ=1/δν they agree again. This is a deduction from the stipulated spectrum, not a fit to Ezekiel's two- or three-line source. Finite individual linewidths eventually damp these revivals.
For a quantitative version of the experiment, the visibility law suggests explicit controls. Measure each arm separately at every coarse delay, subtract the detector's dark signal and any measured background, then normalize by 2I1​I2​​/(I1​+I2​). Keep the returning beams aligned on the same detector region with parallel linear polarizations; keep detector gain fixed and avoid saturation. Resolve the small mirror scan electrically, rather than averaging over its moving interference fringes. Repeat scans to identify vibration or drift. These controls follow from the averaging and mode-matching assumptions in first-order optical coherence; loss of contrast alone cannot distinguish source decorrelation from apparatus motion, misalignment or insufficient spatial resolution. The finite travel range gives access only to a finite range of delays.
The practical gain is that wave interference measures field correlations even when the detector cannot follow the optical oscillation itself. A long optical coherence length allows unequal-arm measurements; a short one localizes high contrast near matched delays. The beautiful feature is that both fading and reappearance of interference fringes are sums of the same rotating complex amplitudes.

A proposed source-width control follows directly from this model: illuminate two fixed openings with a distant adjustable luminous slit of full width w at distance R, so Θ≈w/R under the small-angle approximation, and hold d and the spectral selection fixed. Increasing w overlays more mutually incoherent, displaced interference fringe patterns. Restrict the recorded region so the path difference stays small compared with the optical coherence length, and resolve the fringes with the detector. Thus an extended incoherent source can give locally excellent wave interference when the sampled separation is small, and almost none when it is larger. Diffraction grating

Words: 997 Articles: 7
Physical optics OurBigBook.com
A diffraction grating is a periodic optical structure whose repeated slits or grooves direct light into diffraction orders through wave interference. Its beauty is that many individually broad contributions cooperate to select narrow directions: the spacing determines where the principal peaks occur, while the number of illuminated elements determines how sharply they are selected. This makes a diffraction grating useful in a spectrometer, where separating wavelengths spatially lets us examine an optical spectrum. [ref].
Consider a transmission diffraction grating in air, illuminated at normal incidence by a plane wave. Let d be the centre-to-centre slit spacing, λ the wavelength in the surrounding medium, and θ the signed outgoing angle from the forward normal. In Fraunhofer diffraction, where observation directions specify the far-field pattern, adjacent contributions have path difference dsinθ and phase difference δ=2πdsinθ/λ. Their wave amplitudes reinforce whenever δ=2πm, giving dsinθ=mλ. This normal-incidence geometry should be kept distinct from the incident and reflected angle convention in the grating equation below. [ref].
Angular colour separation follows immediately. At fixed nonzero diffraction order, increasing the wavelength moves the peak farther from the normal. With d=2μm, first-order light at 450nm leaves at 13.003∘, whereas 650nm leaves at 18.966∘: a separation of 5.963∘. The zero diffraction order stays at 0∘ for both wavelengths. Thus grating dispersion comes from an orderly dependence of wave interference on wavelength, rather than an arbitrary assignment of colours to directions.
For N identical slits with uniform coherent illumination, meaning stable relative wave phases across the array, the normalized wave interference factor is
FN​(θ)=​N1​∑j=0N−1​eijδ​2=[Nsin(δ/2)sin(Nδ/2)​]2,δ=λ2πdsinθ​.
(88)
The apparent 0/0 at a principal peak has limiting value one. A short explanation uses the geometric series: equal wave phases add N equal complex amplitudes; a small directional change distributes those contributions around the complex plane and allows cancellation. With each slit's contribution held fixed, peak scalar wave intensity scales as N2. The normalized plots remove that height change to make the narrowing visible. Stable relative wave phases, or optical coherence, are essential; a sum of independent intensities would lose this array structure. [ref].
For finite slit width a, the ideal rectangular-slit model multiplies FN​ by a broad single-slit diffraction envelope:
I(0)I(θ)​=[usinu​]2FN​(θ),u=λπasinθ​.
(89)
The sinc function factor, extended continuously at u=0, controls the brightness available to the narrow peaks. For example, a=0.5μm gives envelope values about 0.811, 0.405, and 0.090 at diffraction orders 1, 2, and 3 in the 600nm example. If an envelope zero coincides with an allowed diffraction order, that peak disappears. A permitted direction therefore need not produce a visible bright spot. [ref].
Historically, Joseph von Fraunhofer used fine parallel wires stretched between threaded rods to make diffraction gratings. Kenyon's historical apparatus account describes both this construction and a later reconstruction with visible light. The example makes the governing idea tangible: regular spacing can turn a simple array of obstacles into an instrument for distinguishing wavelengths. [ref].

Fluorescence

Physical optics OurBigBook.com
Fluorescence is photon emission following photon absorption by matter: an excited state releases some of its energy as light. A fluorophore can therefore mark where something is, while its fluorescence emission spectrum and fluorescence lifetime report different aspects of its environment. Fluorescein is one example; FRET exploits a competing route for excitation energy rather than requiring a second emitted photon.
The usual molecular sequence is excitation, relaxation, then emission, as in the Jablonski diagram. The emitted photon commonly has lower energy and longer wavelength, giving a Stokes shift; the exceptions are discussed below.[ref]

A fluorophore is a fluorescent molecule or fluorescent part of a molecule. Its usefulness as a label depends on how efficiently it absorbs the chosen excitation light, its fluorescence quantum yield, and its resistance to photobleaching. A large fluorescence quantum yield alone does not guarantee a bright image if few excitation photons are absorbed or collected.

Jablonski diagram

Words: 176
Fluorescence OurBigBook.com
A Jablonski diagram arranges molecular energy eigenstates vertically and draws arrows for changes between them. In the usual closed-shell molecular example, S0​ is the electronic ground state, S1​ and S2​ are electronic excited states with singlet state spin, and T1​ has triplet state spin. Each electronic state also has levels of molecular vibration. The diagram records possible processes, not molecular paths in space.[ref]
Photon absorption can populate an upper level of molecular vibration in S1​. Relaxation removes excess energy without photon emission; fluorescence commonly starts from relaxed S1​.[ref] The drawing also includes relaxation from a higher electronic excited state and a competing spin-changing route to a triplet state.

Confocal microscopy forms an image by scanning a localized illumination spot and preferentially detecting light from the same small region. Confocal optical sectioning suppresses that haze, revealing structure at a chosen depth without cutting the specimen. The useful idea is a paired selection: where excitation occurs, and which emitted photons reach the photodetector. [ref]
The scope here is single-point, linear fluorescence imaging. Confocal microscopy can also use reflected light; its broader implementations need not all have the same scanning mechanism. The patent Microscopy apparatus, US3013467A, by Marvin Minsky describes a point source imaged onto a specimen, a second pinhole receiving its image, specimen scanning, and a synchronized display. It was filed on 7 November 1957 and published on 19 December 1961; the filing date should not be described as the grant date. This is evidence for that apparatus and those dates, rather than a claim that all later fluorescence instruments were already present in it. [ref]

Modern laser instruments can supply the illumination point with an optical fiber or a suitable focused laser mode instead of a separate metal illumination pinhole. [ref]
A fluorescent emitter at the selected optical focus forms a compact point spread function at the detection aperture. An emitter displaced axially produces a broadened spot there through defocus; a smaller fraction of its collected light passes. The emitter still exists and still emits photons. Rejected photons strike the opaque mask or other parts of the instrument instead of contributing to the accepted detector channel. Neither a finite pinhole nor diffraction makes the accepted out-of-focus contribution exactly zero.

A point spread function is an imaging system's response to an optical point source. Here it means the distribution of image light intensity: an ideal point object becomes a finite spot, often with faint rings, because of diffraction. An unresolved star and a sufficiently small bead emitting fluorescence are practical approximations to an optical point source. Their image tells us how nearby object details will overlap, and reveals blurring from optical aberrations, defocus, and, for an optical telescope, astronomical seeing.
A useful convention separates shape from throughput. At a fixed image plane, let p(x)≥0 be the point spread function with ∫R2​p(x)d2x=1. Its units are inverse area. A point delivering detected radiant flux F at image position x0​ produces light intensity Fp(x−x0​); this point spread function normalization makes the integral over the image equal to F. A profile divided by its own peak is convenient for comparing widths, but is a different point spread function normalization and does not by itself compare total radiant flux.
In incoherent imaging, different object points have negligible mutual spatial optical coherence over the measurement, so their image light intensities add. If the response also obeys translation invariance over the chosen field of view, the expected continuous image is the convolution
I(x)=τ∫R2​O(u)p(x−u)d2u=τ(O∗p)(x).
(102)
Here O is the object brightness distribution expressed in image-scaled coordinates, with magnification already included, and τ is constant transmission. For O(u)=F0​δ(u−u0​), where δ is the two-dimensional Dirac delta function, this gives I=τF0​p(x−u0​). A changing response across the field of view instead requires a position-dependent integral kernel p(x;u); one measured point spread function is then only a local calibration.
In coherent imaging, the superposition principle applies to the complex wave amplitudes. With amplitude spread function h, the corresponding ideal model is
Eimage​=h∗Eobject​,Iimage​=∣Eimage​∣2,p=∫R2​∣h∣2d2x∣h∣2​.
(103)
Thus ∣h∗E∣2 generally differs from ∣h∣2∗∣E∣2: coherent contributions produce wave interference terms that depend on their relative wave phases. Their time average vanishes for mutually incoherent emitters, which explains the intensity convolution. Partial optical coherence requires the correlations between object points as well.[ref]
The figure is an original diffraction model, not measured data. All panels have the same total radiant flux: each member of a pair contributes half the single-source radiant flux. Dashed curves show the separate light intensity contributions; the solid curve is their sum. The point spread functions have tails, so even sources satisfying the Rayleigh criterion overlap. As separation decreases, the image changes continuously; there is no abrupt disappearance of all information at one separation.
A motivating measured example is Measurement of point-spread function (PSF) for confocal fluorescence microscopy by InCheon Song and others (2005). A 543.8nm laser, delivered through an optical fiber, excited fluorescent beads on a slide through a 100×, numerical aperture 1.3 oil-immersion objective. A moving stage scanned the bead; emitted light returned through the objective, an emission filter and a pinhole to a photodiode. The readout was fluorescence light intensity against scanned position. Under the same setup, nominal bead diameters 0.17, 0.5, and 1μm produced progressively broader measured spots. The size comparison controls for the finite object: the measured response is the convolution of bead emission with the effective point spread function, rather than a pure point response. Inverting this convolution model gave a response compared with the theoretical one. The smaller bead gave a weaker signal relative to noise; uncertainty in actual bead diameter also affected the restored width. These are limits of the calibration. In confocal microscopy, excitation and pinhole detection jointly determine the effective point spread function; this experiment does not measure the ideal widefield Airy disk plotted above.[ref]
For a new calibration, useful additional controls are to measure detector background, avoid saturating the photodetector, repeat the scan to check stability, and compare isolated beads at several positions in the field of view. Record wavelength, numerical aperture, pinhole setting, sampling interval and optical focus. These are practical recommendations, not extra measurements claimed for the published experiment.

The Airy disk is the central bright region, up to the first dark ring, in the scalar diffraction pattern of a uniformly illuminated, unobscured circular aperture. The whole pattern includes the weaker surrounding rings; its radius is distinct from its full width at half maximum.

The optical transfer function is the Fourier transform of the normalized intensity point spread function for incoherent imaging with translation invariance, using spatial frequency in cycles per unit length. It has H(0)=1. For an ideal circular pupil it is the normalized pupil autocorrelation, with cutoff 2NA/λ0​ in object coordinates: no overlap remains when two pupil copies are shifted apart by more than one pupil diameter.[ref]

A diffraction-limited system has an optical response close to the ideal diffraction response for its specified optical pupil, wavelength and optical focus. Improving the optical aberrations further makes little difference to that response. This describes the optics: a poorly sampled or noisy detector can still deliver an image with much worse usable diffraction-limited resolution.
The optical pupil determines which wave amplitudes and wave phases contribute to an image point. In a scalar, paraxial approximation at the focal plane of an optical lens in air, write the pupil transmission as T(u,v)eiϕ(u,v), after removing the ideal focusing phase. The amplitude spread function is proportional to its scaled Fourier transform:

Here (u,v) are pupil coordinates, (x,y) are image coordinates, f is focal length, and λ is the wavelength in air. For a uniformly transmitting, unobscured circular optical pupil at ideal optical focus, the result is an Airy disk with surrounding rings. A blocked centre, support structures, or nonuniform transmission changes the ideal point spread function; “diffraction limited” does not specify one universal spot shape. The existing Fourier model of a Lyot coronagraph illustrates how pupil and focal masks deliberately alter this response.[ref]
Optical aberrations add pupil wave phase errors. Defocus contributes a quadratic pupil wave phase in the paraxial approximation, redistributing light intensity from the best-focused spot. The Strehl ratio compares the peak with the ideal response for the same pupil and total radiant flux. A broad optical spectrum produces a weighted sum of wavelength-dependent point spread functions; chromatic aberration can additionally change optical focus with wavelength. Finer sampling cannot alone recover spatial frequencies removed by the optics, and Fourier deconvolution amplifies noise where the optical transfer function is small. Photon shot noise, read noise, optical aberrations and defocus can all worsen practical discrimination. A useful resolution claim therefore reports the object model, criterion, wavelength, numerical aperture, sampling and signal-to-noise ratio in photon counting.

Geometrical optics

Words: 6k Articles: 49
Optics OurBigBook.com
Geometrical optics describes propagation by rays and Snell's law, neglecting diffraction on scales much larger than the wavelength.
A light ray is a path in an approximation, not a physical thread of zero width. In a transparent, homogeneous, isotropic medium it is straight and perpendicular to a wavefront; boundaries redirect it by the law of reflection or Snell's law. The approximation is useful when the wavelength is small compared with relevant apertures, surface curvature scales, and distances over which the refractive index changes. For an illustrative wavelength of 500nm and a 10mm aperture, their ratio is 5×10−5. That small ratio supports ray tracing for image location, but does not eliminate diffraction when calculating the fine structure of a focused spot. At a wave caustic, geometrical optics can fail despite large optical elements. [ref].
The mechanism of refraction is a change in phase velocity. For transparent isotropic media at the chosen frequency, the refractive index is
n=vphase​c​,n1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​,
(109)
where c is the vacuum speed of light and the angles are measured from the interface normal vector. At a stationary planar interface the frequency and tangential wavevector match across the boundary. Since the wavenumber is k=nω/c, that matching gives Snell's law. The transmitted wavelength changes while the frequency stays fixed. Here n uses phase velocity, which need not equal group velocity. [ref]. [ref].
Choose model air with n1​=1 and model glass with n2​=1.5, without claiming these are exact values for every sample or wavelength. At θ1​=45∘, Snell's law gives
θ2​=arcsin(1.5sin45∘​)≈28.1255∘.
(110)
The transmitted light ray bends toward the normal vector; its phase velocity is c/1.5, and its wavelength is two thirds of the air value. By reversibility of an optical ray, incidence from glass at 28.1255∘ returns the outgoing air angle 45∘.
Incidence from glass at 45∘ is a different experiment. It would require sinθ2​=1.5sin45∘≈1.06066, so there is no real transmitted angle. The critical angle for total internal reflection is
θc​=arcsin(1/1.5)≈41.8103∘.
(111)
Above this angle, an ideal lossless glass-air boundary produces total internal reflection. The physical optics description still permits an evanescent wave in the air, although no propagating transmitted light ray crosses the boundary. [ref]. [ref].
The usefulness of geometrical optics is that complicated instruments can be assembled from these local rules. Applying Snell's law at successive curved surfaces changes a spreading bundle into a converging one. The Fermat principle unifies the construction through stationary optical path length; stationarity does not require a global minimum. [ref]. Fang's MIT notes explicitly connect this principle to specular reflection, refraction, and thin lens imaging, providing a route from individual paths to complete instruments. [ref].

A wave caustic is a locus where the projection of a family of rays or wavefronts becomes singular. Several ray paths may coalesce there, and the geometrical approximation can predict divergent intensity. Finite-wavelength diffraction replaces that ideal divergence by a resolved wave pattern. The construction applies to acoustic as well as optical waves.

Etendue (G=n2AΩ)

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Geometrical optics OurBigBook.com
Etendue measures how much position-and-direction space a bundle of light rays occupies. A small spot accepting a wide range of directions can have the same etendue as a large spot accepting a narrow range. This makes etendue useful for deciding whether an optical instrument can deliver an extended source's entire admitted radiant flux to a small receiver. For forward crossings of a surface, the geometrical optics definition is
G=∫B​n2cosθdAdΩ,0≤θ<2π​,
(112)
where B is the occupied set of surface positions and directions, n is the local refractive index, dA is actual surface area, dΩ is solid angle, and θ is the angle to the forward unit normal. The cosine supplies the projected area. Opposite crossing directions must be counted separately with positive projected area, rather than cancelling them in a signed integral. [ref]
The shorthand G≃n2AΩ assumes constant refractive index, a narrow nearly normal bundle, and the same admitted directions across the whole area A. At larger angles, use the cosine-weighted integral; a position-dependent angular acceptance cannot generally be replaced by the product of two independent extents.

Conservation of etendue (Gout​=Gin​)

Words: 207 Articles: 1
Etendue OurBigBook.com
Lossless reversible propagation preserves the etendue of the same bundle of light rays. Here the model uses stationary isotropic media, specular reflection and refraction, with every selected light ray reaching the output and with no optical gain or scattering of light. An aperture that blocks some incident light rays changes which bundle is counted; the full incident and transmitted etendue need not be equal. [ref]
The underlying phase space has four coordinates. In a planar section with constant refractive index, let (x,y) locate a light ray and set
px​=nsinθcosϕ,py​=nsinθsinϕ.
(113)
The Jacobian determinant from spherical coordinates gives
dpx​dpy​=n2sinθcosθdθdϕ=n2cosθdΩ,dG=dxdydpx​dpy​.
(114)
Thus etendue is a four-dimensional volume, preserved by the optical counterpart of Liouville theorem in Hamiltonian mechanics. Individual position and direction extents may change, and correlations between them matter. The Lagrange optical invariant is a related paraxial approximation invariant for pairs of light rays, rather than the full four-dimensional measure.

Basic radiance is radiance divided by the square of the refractive index. For radiance L at a fixed wavelength,
dΦ=n2L​dG.

Lossless propagation conserves reduced radiance along each light ray; L itself is conserved only when the endpoint refractive indices agree. A larger irradiance at a smaller image can result from admitting more directions without increasing reduced radiance. Uniform wave absorption can lower radiant flux while leaving the occupied geometric etendue unchanged; an opaque aperture removes part of that occupied set. [ref]

G=n2A∫02π​∫0θmax​​cosθsinθdθdϕ=n2Aπsin2θmax​=πANA2,

where NA=nsinθmax​ is the appropriate side's numerical aperture. The ordinary cone solid angle is 2π(1−cosθmax​); its cosine-weighted value is πsin2θmax​. A full forward hemisphere therefore gives G=n2Aπ, rather than 2πn2A. [ref]

Area-angle tradeoff (n12​A1​sin2θ1​=n22​A2​sin2θ2​)

Etendue OurBigBook.com
When both endpoint bundles have the filled circular-cone geometry of etendue of a circular aperture and cone, conservation of etendue gives
n12​A1​sin2θ1​=n22​A2​sin2θ2​.
(118)
For the same refractive index, quadrupling the area halves the sine of the cone half-angle. In the 10mm, 30∘ example, an ideal output of diameter 20mm must have sinθ2​=1/4, so θ2​≈14.4775∘. Equal bounding area and solid angle do not alone prove equal etendue: an actual output can have unoccupied directions or position-direction correlations. The filled-cone equation is an exact model of the specified bundles and a capacity constraint on an optical instrument, not a guarantee of an aberration-free implementation.

nin2​Ain​πsin2θin​≤nout2​Aout​πsin2θout​.
(120)

C≤nin2​sin2θin​nout2​sin2θout​​≤nin2​sin2θin​nout2​​.

If the output half-angle is restricted to 60∘, C≤3 and the receiver diameter must be at least 10/3​≈5.7735mm. For a receiver medium with model refractive index nout​=1.5, the full-hemisphere capacity bound instead gives C≤9; that larger value also depends on transmitting the bundle into that medium.

(122)
The maximum mean irradiance gain remains ηC≤4. With nonuniform radiance, rejecting a given fraction of geometric etendue need not reject the same fraction of radiant flux.
These bounds use a filled extended-source bundle in passive reversible geometrical optics, comparing the same wavelength and the same radiation channels. An ideal optical point source does not fill that four-dimensional set. Diffraction, optical coherence, or coupling a Gaussian beam into an optical fiber require a physical optics calculation; the cone bound is not a universal guarantee for a single wave mode. Likewise, optical gain or fluorescence changes the propagation assumptions.

Etendue bench measurement

Words: 237
Etendue OurBigBook.com
A proposed optical bench test uses a steady illuminated diffuse patch, a relay made from two optical lens elements, interchangeable centred circular stops, and a calibrated optical power meter large enough to collect the whole output bundle. Start with small cone angles so an ordinary relay approximates the area-angle tradeoff. Measure the patch's image diameter and the accepted angular extent at both conjugate planes; the transverse magnification gives the spatial scale, but does not by itself measure etendue.
Map the local radiance with a baffled photodiode on translation and rotation stages, using two small aligned holes to select a narrow known solid angle. Keep the sampled position fixed while scanning direction, calibrate the sampling footprint and angular response, and repeat at several positions. Numerically integrate n2cosθdAdΩ over the occupied samples, and integrate (L/n2)dG to predict the collected radiant flux. This checks the filled-cone assumption instead of inferring it from two outer dimensions.
Compare the relay without a stop and with a stop of 0.6 times the illuminated diameter in the same plane. The uniform-bundle prediction is a radiant flux ratio of 0.36, with unchanged local radiance in the surviving samples. Cover the input for a dark reading, monitor source drift, repeat the open-stop reading, check detector linearity with calibrated optical attenuators, and enlarge the collecting detector or scan it to check for missed light rays. Lens losses, angular response, illumination gradients, alignment errors and diffraction can spoil the ideal prediction; their effects must be measured separately. This is a procedure to try, with predicted readouts, not purported experimental data.

An optical axis is the reference line through the centres of rotational symmetry of an optical system. A folded system can have successive axis segments related by reflection.

The incident ray, reflected ray and surface normal lie in one plane; incidence and reflection angles measured from the normal are equal. For a unit incident direction d and unit normal n, reflection gives d−2(d⋅n)n.

Geometrical optics OurBigBook.com
In a stationary reciprocal optical medium, reversing the direction of a ray produces a ray along the same path. Snell's law is unchanged when its two media and ray directions are interchanged.

Lens (optics)

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Geometrical optics OurBigBook.com
An optical lens is a transparent element, or assembly of elements, that redirects a bundle of light rays to form images or change how the bundle spreads. In an ordinary glass optical lens, refraction at the surfaces provides the redirection: their changing normal vectors make Snell's law bend different light rays by different amounts. A converging optical lens brings incoming light rays parallel to its optical axis toward an optical focus; a diverging optical lens makes them spread as if from an optical focus on the incoming side. [ref].
For a usual glass thin lens in air, a form thicker at the centre than at the edges normally converges, with positive focal length; one thinner at the centre normally diverges. Shape alone is insufficient: the refractive index relative to the surroundings also matters, as the lensmaker's equation shows. An aperture selects which light rays pass; an optical lens also changes their directions. The distinction explains how an optical camera can gather light from one object point over many incoming directions and deliver it to one image location.
The beautiful simplification is that an entire bundle can be characterized by a focal length, and two constructed light rays can locate an image. The thin lens examples below turn that geometry into a prediction of image position, orientation and transverse magnification. A real optical lens retains optical aberrations and diffraction, so the construction is a useful leading model rather than an exact solution of Maxwell's equations.[ref]
Early mathematical treatments include Johannes Kepler's 1611 Dioptrice, whose title explicitly concerns vision through newly invented instruments using transparent glass, and René Descartes's 1637 La Dioptrique, whose seventh discourse discusses improving vision with shaped glass. These are landmarks in explaining and designing optical instruments, rather than dates for the invention of the optical lens. [ref]; [ref].

Focus (optics, F)

Words: 62
Lens (optics) OurBigBook.com
An optical focus is a point where a specified bundle of light rays converges, or where its backward extensions meet. For a converging thin lens receiving light rays parallel to the optical axis, the rear optical focus is (f,0) when the thin lens is at x=0; its front optical focus is (−f,0). An object's image is generally elsewhere: the optical focus describes the parallel incoming bundle, while the thin lens equation locates the image for a finite object distance.

Focal length (f)

Words: 254 Articles: 2
Lens (optics) OurBigBook.com
The focal length f specifies the signed distance from an ideal thin lens to its optical focus for incident light rays parallel to the optical axis. A converging thin lens has f>0, with a rear optical focus beyond the thin lens; a diverging thin lens has f<0, with a virtual optical focus on the incoming side. The focal length is a property of the optical lens in its specified surroundings, not the image distance for every object. For example, a converging thin lens with f=1m images an object 3m away at 1.5m, as computed below. [ref].
Optical power (Φ=1/f)
Words: 165 Articles: 1
Focal length OurBigBook.com
The optical power is reciprocal signed focal length, Φ=1/f. With f expressed in metres, optical power is expressed in dioptres: f=1m gives Φ=+1D, while f=−0.5m gives Φ=−2D. The sign distinguishes converging and diverging optical lens elements; the magnitude measures how strongly they change the direction of a light ray at a given height. [ref].
For two ideal thin lens elements in contact in air, optical powers add: Φtotal​=Φ1​+Φ2​. Thus +2D and −1D combine to give +1D, or ftotal​=1m. Separation changes the rule: for two ideal thin lens elements separated by d in air, their equivalent optical power is Φ1​+Φ2​−dΦ1​Φ2​. The contact rule is the d=0 case.[ref]

Optical power OurBigBook.com
A dioptre, also spelled diopter, is the unit of optical power equal to one reciprocal metre. In Φ=1/f, convert focal length to metres before taking the reciprocal: f=25cm=0.25m gives Φ=4D, not 0.04D. A dioptre measures focusing strength, distinct from the transverse magnification of an image.

Thin lens (1/u+1/v=1/f)

Words: 851 Articles: 2
Lens (optics) OurBigBook.com
A thin lens models an optical lens by collapsing its refracting surfaces into one plane, neglecting thickness relative to the relevant radius of curvature values and object and image distances. Here use an ideal converging thin lens in air and the paraxial approximation: light rays make small angles with the optical axis, so Snell's law can be linearized using the small-angle approximation. Equal surrounding refractive indices on both sides give the familiar symmetric equation.[ref]
Put the thin lens at x=0, with incident light travelling to the right. An object at x=−u has u>0. The image coordinate is x=v: v>0 for a real image and v<0 for a virtual image. The converging thin lens has focal length f>0, and heights ho​,hi​ are signed relative to the optical axis. The thin lens equation and transverse magnification are
f1​=u1​+v1​,v=u−ffu​,m=ho​hi​​=−uv​.
(123)
The expression for v requires u=f. Negative transverse magnification means inverted; positive transverse magnification means upright. Remember that the positive distance u differs in sign from the object's coordinate −u. [ref].
For focal length f=1m, object distance u=3m, and object height ho​=0.1m, calculation gives
v1​=(1−31​)m−1=32​m−1,v=1.5m,m=−0.5,hi​=−0.05m.
(124)
The real image is inverted, half as tall, and located 1.5m to the right of the thin lens. A screen at that position receives the image because the outgoing light rays actually meet there.
For the same focal length f=1m and object height ho​=0.1m, move the object inside the front optical focus, to u=0.5m. Then
v1​=(1−2)m−1=−1m−1,v=−1m,m=2,hi​=0.2m.
(125)
The virtual image is upright, twice as tall, and apparently 1m to the left of the thin lens. Outgoing light rays still travel to the right; only their backward extensions intersect at the virtual image. A screen there cannot collect that image from the outgoing bundle. This geometry explains why a converging optical lens can act as a magnifier when held close to an object. [ref].
Both diagrams use two rules for ray tracing. A light ray from the object's tip parallel to the optical axis reaches the thin lens at (0,ho​) and exits along the straight line through the rear optical focus (f,0). Another light ray through the centre (0,0) continues undeviated in the ideal thin lens model. Their intersection, or the intersection of their backward extensions, locates the image tip. [ref].
A short geometric proof outline makes the signs transparent. The two outgoing straight lines are
yparallel​(x)=ho​(1−fx​),ycentre​(x)=−uho​​x.
(126)
For nonzero ho​, equating their heights at x=v gives 1−v/f=−v/u, hence the thin lens equation; the centre light ray gives hi​/ho​=−v/u, hence the transverse magnification. This derives the image equations from the ideal ray tracing rules, whose physical justification comes from Snell's law in the paraxial approximation.
At u=f, the two outgoing straight lines are parallel: there is no finite image position. For u>f the real image has m<0; for 0<u<f the virtual image has m>0. These cases let an optical camera designer choose a receiving position and let a user understand a magnifier. An actual optical lens has finite apertures, which cause diffraction and impose diffraction-limited resolution; optical aberrations can further blur the image. The diagrams are ideal geometrical optics, with exact coordinates within that model, rather than exact predictions of Maxwell's equations. [ref].

For fixed object-screen separation L>4f, a converging thin lens focuses at two positions separated by d=L2−4Lf​. Thus f=(L2−d2)/(4L). The method finds focal length without needing to locate a thin lens's optical center precisely.
Lensmaker's equation
Words: 181
Thin lens OurBigBook.com
The lensmaker's equation connects focal length to the refractive index and shape of a thin lens. For a thin lens in air with surfaces shaped as parts of spheres, refractive index n, and incident light travelling to the right,
f1​=(n−1)(Ra​1​−Rb​1​).
(127)
Each signed radius of curvature is positive when its centre of curvature lies to the right of that surface, and negative when it lies to the left. A symmetric biconvex thin lens with n=1.5, Ra​=1m, and Rb​=−1m therefore has 1/f=0.5(1+1)m−1=1m−1, giving f=1m and optical power +1D. This is an ideal shape example consistent with the thin lens diagrams, not a specification of their finite thickness.
In a uniform surrounding medium of refractive index ns​ on both sides, replace n−1 by n/ns​−1. Thus the same shape reverses its focusing sign if its refractive index is lower than its surroundings: for n=1.5 and ns​=2, the same radii give 1/f=−0.5m−1, or f=−2m. Positive focal length therefore cannot be inferred from convex shape in every environment. A proof outline applies Snell's law with the small-angle approximation at each surface, adds their direction changes, and neglects the distance between them. [ref].

Optical aberration

Words: 3k Articles: 15
Geometrical optics OurBigBook.com
An optical aberration is a departure from ideal image formation: light rays from one object point may miss their intended common image point, or image positions may depart from the intended mapping. Spherical aberration, coma, and astigmatism describe different ways of spreading a point's light rays; optical distortion can change image shape without spreading each point. In physical optics, these departures can be described by wavefront error relative to a reference wavefront. Diffraction also gives a finite point spread function in a perfect optical instrument, so an extended image alone does not establish an optical aberration.

Seidel aberration

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Optical aberration OurBigBook.com
The five Seidel aberrations of a rotationally symmetric optical system are spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature, and optical distortion.
Spherical aberration
Words: 32
Seidel aberration OurBigBook.com
Spherical aberration makes rays at different pupil radii focus at different axial positions. Its primary pupil dependence is quartic; the balanced Zernike spherical mode also contains quadratic and constant terms to remove defocus and piston.
Coma (optics)
Words: 1k Articles: 2
Seidel aberration OurBigBook.com
Coma makes an off-axis optical point source appear asymmetric, often with a compact head and a flaring tail like a comet. Different parts of the optical pupil send its light rays to different transverse image positions. A sharp central star image therefore does not guarantee sharp images across an optical telescope's field of view. In an idealized, aligned system with rotational symmetry, coma vanishes on the optical axis; misalignment can introduce coma even at the nominal field centre.[ref]
Coma differs from spherical aberration, whose dependence on optical pupil radius can blur an on-axis point without selecting a transverse direction. Astigmatism gives different optical foci in two perpendicular sections of an off-axis bundle; a through-focus sequence can change its elongated image's orientation. Diffraction persists when these optical aberrations vanish. A real asymmetric point spread function may mix several effects, so its appearance alone is not a unique diagnosis of coma.
The classical primary description belongs to the nineteenth-century Seidel aberration classification of five primary monochromatic image errors.[ref] It remains useful in modern design: OpticStudio's Seidel Coefficients by ANSYS, Inc. documentation lists coma as W131​ and tabulates each surface's contribution as well as the system sum (Discussion). Cancellation of contributions can reduce coma without making every surface individually free of it. The same documentation limits this calculation to specified systems with axially symmetric surfaces; higher-order terms and broken rotational symmetry require more general ray tracing.
Seidel coma pupil mapping (w=hρ3cosθ)
Words: 537
Coma (optics) OurBigBook.com
Consider an original, explicitly normalized model of primary coma, rather than a prescription for a particular optical lens. Let (u,v) be Cartesian coordinates in a circular optical pupil divided by its radius a, with u2+v2≤1. Let h=α/α0​ be a signed small field angle divided by an arbitrary positive reference angle. With polar coordinates u=ρcosθ, v=ρsinθ, prescribe the wavefront error
W(u,v)=W0​w(u,v),w(u,v)=hρ3cosθ=hu(u2+v2).
(128)
Here W0​ is an arbitrary positive optical path difference scale, not a measured error. The cubic optical pupil dependence and linear field dependence are the classical Seidel form.[ref]
In the paraxial approximation, light ray direction errors follow the transverse gradient of wavefront error. For a reference sphere a distance L from the exit optical pupil in a uniform image medium of refractive index n, the corresponding image-error scale is s=LW0​/(na). Choose image-error coordinate signs so the normalized displacement is ∇w; reversing the convention reverses the plotted orientation. Image coordinates below are errors relative to the ideal image of this particular object point, rather than positions of different objects:
X=∂u∂w​=h(3u2+v2),Y=∂v∂w​=2huv.
(129)
The partial derivatives explain the asymmetry: opposite optical pupil points (u,v) and (−u,−v) land together, rather than on opposite sides of the ideal image. For h>0, every X is nonnegative, while Y can have either sign. The figures stipulate this single wavefront error, omit other optical aberrations and diffraction, and assign no instrument dimensions.
For a ring of fixed optical pupil radius ρ, the double-angle formulas for trigonometric functions give
X=hρ2(2+cos2θ),Y=hρ2sin2θ,(X−2hρ2)2+Y2=h2ρ4.
(130)
Thus each ring maps into a circle of radius ∣h∣ρ2 whose centre is displaced by 2hρ2. Doubling ρ quadruples both sizes; for h=1, the edge ring has centre (2,0) and radius 1, while the half-radius ring has centre (1/2,0) and radius 1/4. Superposing these displaced circles produces the comet-like envelope.
For uniform irradiance over the circular optical pupil, equal area samples give an equal-weight geometrical image. Its centroid is (h,0) because ⟨u2⟩=⟨v2⟩=1/4 and ⟨uv⟩=0. Moving the coordinate origin to that centroid translates the image; it does not remove its asymmetric shape. Adding a linear term to w likewise translates all light rays equally. These origin choices must be distinguished from changing the optical aberration itself.
The model's full transverse extent is 3∣h∣ along X and 2∣h∣ along Y. Halving the field angle halves the blur, and reversing it reverses the pattern about the ideal image. This isolates why coma matters for an optical camera's usable field of view: collecting more light does not ensure that off-axis points remain compact. Near diffraction-limited resolution, a physical optics calculation of the point spread function is needed instead of interpreting the geometrical tip as an infinitely sharp image.[ref]
Off-axis pinhole test for coma
Words: 321
Coma (optics) OurBigBook.com
The institution-issued AY 105 Lab Experiment 3: Optical aberrations by California Institute of Technology (Spring 2011 offering, Part A, pp. 2–3, 7–8) specifies a concrete optical bench: a lamp, opal diffuser and condensing optical lens illuminate a 25 or 30μm optical pinhole; a photographic telephoto optical lens acts as a collimator, producing an approximately 75mm beam. A test optical lens sits on a rotation stage, followed by an adjustable optical microscope. The procedure establishes the on-axis image, then rotates the test optical lens a few degrees and examines the off-axis image through optical focus. It compares this readout with through-focus ray tracing at the corresponding field angles and offers a Ronchi ruling to calibrate the measuring eyepiece.
Part B (pp. 9–10) substitutes a spherical mirror of 1m radius of curvature, with the optical microscope beside the incoming beam so the image is necessarily off-axis. It calls for measuring the field angle, calibrating the eyepiece and recording the image's length and width at minimum size. These are specified apparatus dimensions and instructions, not supplied measurement results or dimensions of the normalized figures.
A controlled extension would record images at zero and equal positive and negative field angles, repeat zero afterwards, and scan through optical focus at every setting. Keep the illuminated optical pupil and illumination fixed, recenter the optical microscope without clipping the bundle, and use its calibrated scale to separate a mere image displacement from a change in blur shape. The pure Seidel coma pupil mapping predicts reversal and linear growth; a stationary asymmetric central image instead calls for checking alignment. A focus-dependent change between perpendicular elongations suggests an astigmatism contribution. These comparisons test the model rather than assuming every off-axis flare is pure coma.
The optical pinhole has finite angular size, approximately its diameter divided by the collimator's focal length; the collimator and observing optical microscope also contribute their own optical aberrations. A broadband lamp can mix chromatic aberration with the geometric blur, and diffraction limits the smallest visible structure. A narrow spectral band, repeated field settings and a reference image help separate these effects. Consequently a measured length and width are useful checks on off-axis image formation, but they cannot by themselves determine a unique coma coefficient or recover the full point spread function.

Chromatic aberration

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Optical aberration OurBigBook.com
An optical camera can focus a white object sharply in one colour while leaving coloured fringes around its edges in another. Chromatic aberration is the dependence of image position or image scale on wavelength, caused by optical dispersion in the optical lens materials. Axial chromatic aberration separates the optical foci along the optical axis; lateral chromatic aberration changes the transverse magnification with wavelength. Moving the receiving plane can favour one colour without bringing all colours into focus. [ref]; [ref].
For ordinary optical glass in the visible range, the blue refractive index exceeds the red refractive index. For a fixed positive thin lens in air, the lensmaker's equation then gives
Φ(λ)=f(λ)1​=[n(λ)−1](Ra​1​−Rb​1​),nblue​>nred​ ⟹ Φblue​>Φred​>0,fblue​<fred​.
(131)
Here λ is wavelength, n is refractive index, Φ is optical power, f is focal length, and Ra​,Rb​ are the signed surface radius of curvature values in the lensmaker's equation. The blue light rays therefore bend more strongly and meet sooner. This ordering is a statement about ordinary visible optical dispersion, not a universal rule for every material and every spectral range. [ref].
For a worked example, take a single positive thin lens with reference optical power Φd​=5D and Abbe number Vd​=60, hence reference focal length fd​=0.2m. Its F–C optical power difference is ΔΦ=ΦF​−ΦC​=Φd​/Vd​=5/60D≈0.08333D, by the achromatic doublet power balance relation below. This difference alone does not locate the reference optical power within the F–C interval. To draw a transparent example, introduce a synthetic colour coordinate q, a dimensionless quantity, with red q=−1/2, reference q=0, and blue q=+1/2, and choose the toy optical dispersion model
Φ(q)=Φd​(1+Vd​q​),f(q)=Φ(q)1​.
(132)
The diagram's red and blue endpoints represent the C and F endpoints of this toy model. Its reference point is placed symmetrically in optical power by construction; q is not a measured wavelength scale, and the model is not measured optical glass data. The endpoint focal lengths are
fred​=5(1−1/120)1​m=11924​m≈0.201681m,fblue​=5(1+1/120)1​m=12124​m≈0.198347m.
(133)
Thus the axial chromatic aberration in this example separates the endpoint optical foci by about 3.334mm. A single receiving plane cannot coincide with both optical foci.
The useful design idea is to cancel changes of optical power while retaining a positive total optical power. An achromatic lens does this with materials having different Abbe numbers. It greatly reduces chromatic aberration, but correcting two chosen wavelengths still leaves the possibility of a secondary spectrum.
Axial chromatic aberration (f(λ))
Words: 34
Chromatic aberration OurBigBook.com
Axial chromatic aberration, also called longitudinal chromatic aberration, is colour-dependent focus position along the optical axis. For incident light rays parallel to the optical axis, it appears as a changing focal length. The chromatic aberration diagram isolates this effect using an ideal thin lens at each colour.
Lateral chromatic aberration (m(λ))
Words: 48
Chromatic aberration OurBigBook.com
Lateral chromatic aberration, also called transverse chromatic aberration, is colour-dependent image scale: an object away from the optical axis can have different image heights at different wavelengths. Its changing transverse magnification produces displaced coloured edges. The on-axis parallel bundle in the chromatic aberration diagram illustrates axial chromatic aberration, and does not measure lateral chromatic aberration. [ref].
Achromatic lens
Words: 884 Articles: 3
Chromatic aberration OurBigBook.com
An achromatic lens combines optical lens elements with different optical dispersion so that two specified wavelengths have the same focal length in the paraxial approximation. This brings their parallel incoming light rays to a common optical focus, helping an optical camera form a sharper image under mixed-colour illumination. A common implementation is an achromatic doublet: a positive crown glass element paired with a negative flint glass element. [ref].
The achromatic doublet does not require either material to have zero optical dispersion. Instead, the positive element gains positive optical power toward blue, while the negative element becomes more negative. Suitable Abbe numbers and signed optical powers let these changes cancel even though their reference optical powers do not cancel. For example, the achromatic doublet power balance calculation below combines +10D with −5D to obtain +5D, or focal length 0.2m, with zero primary F–C optical power difference. The smaller Abbe number of the negative element makes its weaker reference optical power sufficient to oppose the positive element's colour change.
An achromatic lens is corrected at two chosen wavelengths, not necessarily at every wavelength between them. The remaining focal length variation is the secondary spectrum. Correcting axial chromatic aberration also does not automatically remove lateral chromatic aberration throughout an imaging system, spherical aberration, or diffraction. Actual designs therefore need ray tracing with the intended wavelengths, element thicknesses, separations and apertures. [ref]; [ref].
Achromatic doublet
Words: 47
Achromatic lens OurBigBook.com
An achromatic doublet is an achromatic lens with two optical lens elements. In the contact thin lens model, their optical powers add and their primary colour changes cancel according to achromatic doublet power balance. The conventional positive achromatic doublet uses a converging crown glass element and a weaker diverging flint glass element; these names describe a common choice, not a universal ordering of every modern optical glass composition.
Achromatic doublet power balance
Words: 575
Achromatic lens OurBigBook.com
Achromatic doublet power balance chooses two signed optical powers to meet two goals: obtain the required focal length and cancel the primary F–C colour difference. Model two thin lens elements in contact in air, using the paraxial approximation. Let i=c,f label the crown glass and flint glass elements, and let Φi,d​ denote each element's optical power at the reference d line. The Abbe number for each material is
Vi​=ni,F​−ni,C​ni,d​−1​.
(134)
The subscripts label standard spectral lines: blue F near 486.1nm, red C near 656.3nm, and reference d near 587.6nm. These are three specified wavelengths, not colour bands. A larger Abbe number means less relative optical dispersion between F and C. [ref].
For a fixed thin lens shape in air, write the lensmaker's equation as Φi​(λ)=Ki​[ni​(λ)−1], with signed shape factor Ki​=1/Ri,a​−1/Ri,b​. Subtracting its C value from its F value gives the primary optical power difference
ΔΦi​=Φi,F​−Φi,C​=Ki​(ni,F​−ni,C​)=Vi​Φi,d​​.
(135)
The negative element has negative ΔΦi​: its blue optical power is more negative, not less negative. The contact rule for optical power therefore gives
Φd​=Φc,d​+Φf,d​=fd​1​,ΔΦtotal​=Vc​Φc,d​​+Vf​Φf,d​​=0.
(136)
This zero is equality of the total F and C optical powers, hence equality of their focal lengths when the total optical power is nonzero. The relation follows directly from the lensmaker's equation and the Abbe number; it is exact within the fixed-shape contact thin lens model. [ref]. Tatum uses a yellow D-line reference; here the Abbe number convention uses the d line consistently.
For a toy design, choose Vc​=60, Vf​=30, Φc,d​=10D and Φf,d​=−5D. Then
Φd​=(10−5)D=5D,fd​=5m−11​=0.2m,ΔΦtotal​=(6010​−305​)D=0.
(137)
The positive element contributes +1/6D to the F–C difference and the negative element contributes −1/6D. This retains the same reference focal length as the single 5D, Vd​=60 thin lens in chromatic aberration, while cancelling its primary colour split. The values are illustrative design parameters, not a catalogue optical glass pair.
Use the same synthetic colour coordinate q=−1/2,0,+1/2 and toy optical dispersion as in chromatic aberration. The two element optical powers and their sum become
Φc​(q)=10(1+60q​)D,Φf​(q)=−5(1+30q​)D,Φtotal​(q)=(5+q[6010​−305​])D=5D.
(138)
At the red endpoint, the element optical powers are 9.916667D and −4.916667D; at the blue endpoint, they are 10.083333D and −5.083333D. Both sums are 5D. In this first-order toy model alone, the sum is constant for every q and the focal length remains 0.2m throughout. Real material optical dispersion is not captured by these two straight slopes, so the flat line is not a claim that a real achromatic doublet focuses all colours perfectly.
For specified nonzero reference optical power Φd​ and distinct Abbe numbers, solving the two balance equations gives
Φc,d​=Vc​−Vf​Φd​Vc​​,Φf,d​=−Vc​−Vf​Φd​Vf​​.
(139)
Thus Φd​>0 and Vc​>Vf​>0 require positive crown glass optical power and negative flint glass optical power. If the two finite Abbe numbers were equal, cancellation would force zero total optical power. If they are close, the required element optical powers become large compared with the total: cancelling primary colour can demand much stronger individual elements.
The contact assumption matters. For two thin lens elements separated by distance s in air, the equivalent optical power is Φc​+Φf​−sΦc​Φf​, evaluated at each wavelength; its colour change need not satisfy the contact balance. Finite thickness, departures from the paraxial approximation, and the secondary spectrum also limit the simple prediction.[ref]
Secondary spectrum
Words: 60
Achromatic lens OurBigBook.com
The secondary spectrum is residual chromatic aberration after an achromatic lens brings two selected wavelengths to the same optical focus. For example, equal red and blue focal lengths can coexist with a different green focal length. The Abbe number fixes one F–C relative difference, not the complete shape of optical dispersion between or beyond those wavelengths. The perfectly flat sum in the achromatic doublet power balance diagram deliberately omits this residual effect. [ref].

For a homogeneous optical prism in air, with apex angle ϕ and refractive index n>1, minimum deviation occurs at the symmetric ray path. Then both internal angles are ϕ/2 and both external angles are (γmin​+ϕ)/2, so Snell's law gives

Measuring the deviation therefore determines the refractive index at the chosen wavelength.

Focal ratio (F=f/D)

Words: 512
Optical instrument OurBigBook.com
The focal ratio, or f-number, of a converging optical instrument focused at infinity is the dimensionless quantity
N=F=Df​,
(141)
where f>0 is effective focal length and D is the on-axis entrance pupil diameter. The notation f/4 means N=4, not f=4 in a particular unit. A 100mm focal length with D=25mm gives f/4. Closing the aperture stop until D=12.5mm gives f/8 while retaining the same focal length. The mechanical opening need not equal D. [ref].
For a thin lens in air with a circular aperture stop at the thin lens, the converging bundle from a distant on-axis point has half-angle α satisfying
tanα=2fD​=2N1​,α≃2N1​in radians.
(142)
The last step uses the small-angle approximation. For a compound optical lens, the cone is set by the image-side optical pupil and its distance from the receiving plane; the simple triangle is not an exact high-angle rule. At finite object distance a thin lens instead gives v=f(1+∣m∣), by its imaging equation and transverse magnification, so its working cone corresponds to v/D=N(1+∣m∣). Nominal focal ratio therefore does not alone specify close-range image irradiance. [ref].
Two useful scalings follow under stated conditions. For a fixed uniform incident beam and unchanged transmission, collected radiant flux scales as D2. For an extended source with fixed radiance, the central image irradiance scales approximately as N−2 in the paraxial approximation: the solid angle of the cone scales as (D/f)2. For an ideal uniformly illuminated unobscured circular entrance pupil, the first dark ring of the point spread function has angular radius and focal plane radius
θ1​≃1.22Dλ​,r1​≃fθ1​=1.22λN.
(143)
Here λ is wavelength. These are first-zero radii, not diameters or a universal rule for resolving arbitrary objects. A proof outline evaluates the circular aperture's Fraunhofer diffraction using its Fourier transform, then uses the first zero of the resulting Bessel function. [ref].
At λ=0.55μm, the example's f/4 and f/8 first-ring radii are 2.684 and 5.368μm. Closing the aperture stop halves D, quarters collected radiant flux and doubles this diffraction radius. It can also reduce optical aberrations by excluding outer light rays; actual sharpness reflects both effects. This explains why a smaller aperture need not produce a sharper image. [ref].
A proposed optical bench check puts a fixed collimator before a converging thin lens and a photodetector large enough to collect the entire image behind it. Compare two centred aperture stops of known diameters while fixing source output, detector gain and integration time. The integrated signal tests the D2 collection law; a spatially resolved optical camera at the focal plane can separately measure the point spread function. Repeat a dark reading and the first aperture stop, and check that neither the incoming beam nor detector clips either bundle. A resolved pinhole source, imperfect collimation, optical aberrations and detector pixel size can dominate the apparent spot width; a single peak reading does not measure total collected radiant flux.

A companion or extended source contributes to the stellar reference used in differential imaging. Subtracting that reference removes part of the desired signal and distorts its shape, photometry or astrometry. Artificial-source injection and forward modelling can estimate the throughput loss.
